For instance, this poor man died at the age of one hundred and twenty years and five days; therefore, the flaw in the reasoning <note>regarding long life always equaling wealth</note> should be understood as quite small. Thus, the inconsistency of this flaw has been demonstrated. Because of this impossibility, these two *Shalini* verses are not considered to be the work of Varahamihira. The reason the Teacher <note>Varahamihira</note> might set aside his own previously shown method of longevity to accept the opinion of Satya is to align with the consensus of many other teachers. As was stated previously in the Teacher’s own declaration on longevity: "Astrology is a traditional science; in cases of contradiction, it is not proper for us to simply choose according to our own will, but rather I shall state the opinion of the many."

Now, someone might say: "Surely this combination you have shown is not *Kemadruma* <note>a specific planetary combination signifying extreme poverty</note> at all." For the Teacher himself will say: "If a planet is in a quadrant from the Moon, or associated with it, *Kemadruma* is not recognized." Since the Moon here is in the seventh house from the Ascendant (a quadrant), this is not *Kemadruma*. To this we reply: Here, the Moon is not counted because the combination must be formed by another planet in relation to the Moon. If you ask how a planet in a quadrant from the Ascendant acts, it is said: because the Ascendant and the Moon are considered equal. As Yavaneshwara <note>Lord of the Greeks/Ionians, an early authority on Indian astrology</note> says: "One should know the Body, the Ascendant, and the Moon as the same." And here Gargi says: "If there are no planets (excluding the Sun) in the 2nd, 12th, or quadrants from the Moon; or if there are no planets in the quadrants from the Ascendant (excluding the Moon), that combination is called *Kemadruma* and is considered despicable. Those born under it follow blamed customs and are joined with poverty and disease." Therefore, even with the Moon in the seventh from the Ascendant, the *Kemadruma* nature of this combination is indeed proven. || 8 ||

### Vernacular Translation—
In the combination where a full lifespan is predicted, other teachers have assumed a "Universal Emperor" (*Chakravartitva*) yoga because six planets are in exaltation. But there is a visible flaw in their opinion: even a completely penniless man can live out a full lifespan. || 8 ||

### Special Meaning—
The essence of this verse is—when a full lifespan is only predicted when planets are exalted, and that same state creates a "Universal Emperor" combination, then whoever is long-lived should also be a universal king or fully wealthy. But this is not observed. Many long-lived people are indeed poor. Therefore, the longevity calculations of Maya, Yavana, and others are inconsistent. Here Bhattotpala says: "According to the previously mentioned views of Maya and Yavana, using the rule 'half in debilitation,' a long-life (full life) combination can occur even in places other than exaltation, where a *Kemadruma* (poverty) combination also exists; thus, one can have a full life and still be poor. Therefore, it appears that this verse is not by Varahamihira, but has been <insert>interpolated</insert> <note>original: "prakshipta"</note> by someone else."

# Chapter on Longevity in the Brihat Jataka

Mercury's longevity 7 years, 0 months; Jupiter's longevity 12 years, 0 months, 11 days, 15 minutes; Venus's longevity 16 years, 2 months, 26 days, 30 minutes; Saturn's longevity 13 years, 4 months, 0 days; Ascendant's longevity 6 years, 0 months. <margin>Therefore, it is proven inconsistent to find fault in the methods of calculating longevity provided by Maya and others. ||8||</margin>

Now, the author describes the longevity according to the opinions of Jivasharma and Satyacharya using the *Aupachhandasika* meter:

**Jivasharma indeed states, according to his own view, that the planetary contribution to the maximum lifespan is one-seventh. The statement of Satyacharya, which equates the years to the number of Navamshas <note>A 1/9th division of a zodiac sign</note> passed by the planet, attains great consistency. ||9||**

Regarding "According to his own view": The teacher named Jivasharma, in his own doctrine, states that the contribution of each planet to the maximum lifespan—which is 120 years and 5 days—is one-seventh part. The word "indeed" is used here to indicate a well-known tradition. To illustrate: The maximum lifespan is 120 years, 0 months, and 5 days. Dividing this by seven, we obtain 17 years, 1 month, 22 days, 8 minutes, and 34 seconds. Just as other teachers have prescribed specific years for the Sun and other planets when in their highest exaltation (such as nineteen, fifteen, etc.), Jivasharma prescribes these "one-seventh of maximum life" years for each planet. The rule "it decreases by half at the lowest point" also applies here; thus, at the point of maximum debilitation, the value is half: 8 years, 6 months, 26 days, 4 minutes, and 17 seconds. For a planet situated between these points, the longevity should be calculated using the Rule of Three <note>A mathematical proportion: if X gives Y, what does Z give?</note> as previously described. Here too, except for retrograde planets, a planet in an enemy's sign loses one-third of its contribution. Except for Venus and Saturn, a planet that is combust <note>Too close to the sun to be seen</note> (excluding Mars) loses half. The reductions for planetary positions in specific houses (half, third, etc.) also apply here. If a malefic planet is in the Ascendant, there is a reduction based on the portion of the sign that has risen. In all these matters, Jivasharma's method is identical to that of other teachers. As Jivasharma says: "Seventeen (17), one (1), twenty-two (22), eight (8), and thirty-four (34) are the years for the lords of the planets when in exaltation. For those in debilitation, it is half. For those in between, the calculation is by proportion; all other remaining calculations should be performed by those skilled in mathematics just as in the *Pinda Ayurdaya* system." Here, the method of calculation is shown for easy understanding.

# Commentary in Language and Sanskrit by Bhattotpala

> 'Subtract the planet's exaltation point from the planet's position. If the remainder is more than six signs, subtract it from the full circle <note>original: "Bhamandala" (360 degrees)</note>. Multiply those degrees by 8641 <gloss>8641</gloss> and divide by 504 <gloss>504</gloss>. The result is the longevity in days according to Jivasharman. Divide the days by thirty for months, and months by twelve for years.'

This is not merely a planet's contribution to longevity; it is a specific fraction. Therefore, he said— "according to his own opinion." By this, he implies: "I have not seen this method in any works of the Rishis <note>Ancient seers</note> or previous Teachers." Thus, this method of longevity is Jivasharman's own invention, which is its flaw. In the scriptures, longevity is explained according to the consensus of all Teachers. Here, the Author <note>Varahamihira</note> has presented the opinions of others, such as Maya, Yavana, Manittha, Shakti, and others. However, in the scripture composed by Yavaneshwara <note>Lord of the Greeks/Ionians</note>, such a method of longevity is not seen. For Yavaneshwara said:
> 'Longevity is derived from the sum of signs and portions of signs.'

To this, it is said that another scripture was composed by Yavaneshwara Sphujidhvaja. As Sphujidhvaja says:
> 'Adding one hundred and fifty to the elapsed number... the era of the Shakas <note>The Shaka Era, starting 78 CE</note> is 1044 <gloss>1044</gloss>; subtracting that, the years elapsed are known.'

Thus, the work of Sphujidhvaja is known to be recent, from the Shaka era. There was another work composed by the earlier Yavana Teachers, and regarding that, Sphujidhvaja also says:
> 'The Yavanas said: The classifications of directions, births, and castes mentioned in the Compendium by the ancients for the planets...'

From this, it is understood that Varahamihira presented the opinion of the *earlier* Yavana Teachers, which we have not seen. Having seen only the work of Sphujidhvaja, the same applies to Parashara. We have only seen the *Parashara Samhita* <note>A treatise on omens and astronomy</note>, not his *Jataka* <note>Natal astrology</note>. It is heard that Parashara composed a work in three branches <note>The three divisions of Jyotisha: Samhita, Hora, and Ganita</note>; for that reason, Varahamihira mentions "Shakti and others" <note>Shakti was the father of Parashara</note>:
> 'Leaving aside Chitra, Parashara speaks of that which brings misfortune to women...'

Such works by Maya and Manittha exist in the science of *Hora* <note>Natal astrology</note>. As Maya says:
> 'The Sun gives nineteen years, the Moon twenty-five. Mars gives fifteen, Mercury twelve when in exaltation. Jupiter gives the same as Mars <note>15</note>, the Preceptor of the Daityas <note>Venus</note> gives twenty-one. The Son of the Sun <note>Saturn</note> gives twenty when in highest exaltation. This longevity is halved when the planet is in its sign of fall; for positions in between, the calculation should be made by proportion.'

And as Manittha says:
> 'Nine, five, two, eight, twelve, five, and one <note>This refers to specific numerical codes for years</note> are the years for the Sun and others in their exaltation signs. In their signs of fall, half these years are given; elsewhere, it must be calculated by proportion. The rule for longevity is also equal to the signs and portions of the hour-sign <note>Ascendant</note> passed.'

Now, Varahamihira’s own opinion on longevity, which follows the views of Yavaneshwara and Satyacharya, is explained: "Equal to the number of Navamshas <note>Ninth-parts of a sign</note> traversed by the planet." In whatever sign and in whichever ninth-part a planet is situated, that ninth-part—counting from Aries—corresponds to the number of years the planet contributes to longevity. This is what was said...

# Chapter on Longevity in the Brihat Jataka
<page-num>168</page-num>

It occurs thus: starting from Aries, a planet grants as many years as the number of <term>Navamshas</term> <note>a one-ninth division of a zodiac sign, equal to 3 degrees and 20 minutes</note> it has traversed. In this way, the years are equal to the number of Navamshas occupied by the planet. To find the months and days, one must perform a <term>Rule of Three</term> <note>a mathematical proportion</note> calculation based on the portion of the current Navamsha already traversed by the planet. The method for this Rule of Three will be explained later. This method of calculating longevity was taught by the preceptor Satyacharya. His statement is as follows:

> "In this system, planets grant longevity in brief based on the combination of signs and Navamshas."

This statement by Satyacharya attains great consistency and is accepted by many preceptors. Likewise, Yavaneshwara states:

> "Lifespans result from the combination of the movement through signs and Navamshas."

Regarding the interpretation of these statements by Satyacharya and Yavaneshwara, there is some disagreement. Some explain "from the movement of signs and Navamshas" as follows: a planet grants as many years of life as the number of Navamshas it has traversed within the sign it currently occupies. In this interpretation, the years are determined by the maximum planetary contribution. This interpretation is accepted by Badarayana and others. As Badarayana says:

> "The signs and Navamshas of a planet, multiplied by twelve and nine respectively from the revolutions, and divided by twelve, yield the years, months, days, and minutes in sequence."

The preceptor Varahamihira has expressed this clearly in his *Svalpa Jataka*. Following this, the interpretation of Satyacharya and Yavaneshwara is made: "Lifespans from the combination of movement in signs and Navamshas" refers to the Navamshas of the signs. Regarding the movement through them: in whatever sign a planet is placed, if it is in the Aries Navamsha, it gives one year; in the Taurus Navamsha, it gives two years. Thus, with the increase of subsequent Navamshas, the years increase until twelve years at the end of the Pisces Navamsha. According to the previous interpretation, the mention of "signs" in the statements of Yavaneshwara and Satyacharya would be redundant. Therefore, it must necessarily be calculated by the Navamshas of the signs. || 6 ||

**Vernacular Translation—** The preceptor Jivasharma, according to his own opinion, stated that the longevity granted by all planets in their positions of exaltation is equal to one-seventh of the maximum human lifespan (which is 120 years and 5 days). This one-seventh equals 17 years, 1 month, 22 days, 8 Ghadi, and 34 Pal. However, this is not universally accepted. Therefore, many preceptors follow the statement of Satyacharya: "A planet's contribution to longevity is equal to the number of Navamshas it has traversed." || 6 ||

**Special Meaning—** The intent is this: Jivasharma felt that the longevity contribution of all planets should be equal when in their respective exaltation signs. Therefore, he calculated the years at exaltation as one-seventh of the maximum lifespan, and half of that (8 years, 6 months, 26 days, 4 Ghadi, 17 Pal) at their point of debilitation. For planets in between, the longevity is calculated by proportion (Rule of Three). Furthermore, if a planet is in the <term>Chakrardha</term> <note>the visible hemisphere</note>, or in an enemy's sign, or combust (too close to the sun), or if a malefic planet is in the Ascendant, reductions must be applied as per the rules of "half, third, or quarter reduction." This results in the "clear" or rectified longevity. As per Jivasharma's statement:

# Page 166
## With the Bhattotpala Sanskrit Commentary and Vernacular Explanation

> "Seventeen, one, two-twos <note>original: 'dvi-yama', meaning 22</note>, eight, and four-threes <note>original: 'veda-agni', meaning 34</note> are the values for the planets. For a planet at its highest point <term>Exaltation: the zodiacal sign where a planet is most powerful</term>, the full years are given; at its lowest point <term>Debilitation: the sign opposite to exaltation</term>, it is half. For positions in between, the calculation should be done by proportion. All other remaining steps should be performed by experts in mathematical principles, just as in the Pindayu system."

Likewise, **Satyacharya** states that— the number of Navamshas <term>Navamsha: a 1/9th division of a zodiac sign, equal to 3 degrees and 20 minutes</term> a planet has traversed should be considered as the number of years. If the number exceeds 12, divide by 12 and the remainder is the planet's contribution to the lifespan. The method to find the traversed Navamshas is to convert the planet's position into minutes <note>original: 'kala'</note> and divide by 200, because 200 minutes equals 1 Navamsha. The resulting number (after dividing by 12) gives the years. To find the months, multiply the remaining minutes by 12 and divide by 200; for days, multiply the remainder by 30 and divide by 200; for smaller units <note>Ghati and Pala</note>, multiply by 60, as the Teacher himself will explain in a later verse. (6)

**A reasoned example of Jivasharma's method of lifespan calculation:**
The maximum lifespan is 120 years and 5 days. Converting this into days gives 43,205 days. One-seventh of this — <gloss>43205 / 7</gloss> — is the lifespan value in days for a planet at its highest point (exaltation). From this, a Rule of Three <note>mathematical proportion</note> is established: if for a distance from exaltation of 0 (i.e., 12 signs or 360 degrees) the lifespan is <gloss>43205 / 7</gloss>, then what is it for the desired distance from exaltation?
Result = <gloss>43205 / 7</gloss> X <gloss>Distance from Exaltation in degrees / 360</gloss>

<gloss>8641 X Distance from Exaltation in degrees / 504</gloss> = The planet's lifespan contribution in days and further units. Here, if the distance from exaltation is more than 6 signs, it should be handled accordingly. Because— as a planet moves forward from its lowest point, its lifespan contribution increases until it reaches its maximum at the highest point. From this, the following formula (verse) arises:

> "Subtract the planet from its exaltation; if the result is less than six signs, subtract it from the full circle (12 signs). Multiply those degrees by 8641 and divide by 504. The resulting days and units are the lifespan according to Jivasharma."

**Meaning**— If the difference between the planet and its exaltation point is more than 6, use that; if it is less than 6 signs, subtract it from 12 signs. Convert the remaining signs etc. into degrees, multiply by 8641, and divide by 504 to find the planet's lifespan contribution in days.

For example— In the previous case, the clear position of the Sun is 0s 6° 46' 40". Subtracting this from the Sun's exaltation point (0s 10°), the difference is 0s 3° 10' 20". This is less than 6 signs, so subtracting it from 11 signs <note>The text suggests a calculation relative to the full circle</note> gives 11s 26° 46' 40". Converting this to degrees gives 356° 46' 40". Multiplying this by 8641 gives 3083348° 46' 40", which is then divided by 504...

By dividing, the quotient in days etc. is 6; 11; 45; 20. Converting this into years etc., we get 16 years, 11 months, 27 days, 45 minutes, and 20 seconds. This is the longevity contributed by the Sun. Similarly, for the Moon, because it is combust <note>original: "ast" - disappearing in the Sun's rays</note> with the Sun, half of 16; 1; 56; 44; 13 is taken, resulting in 8; 0; 28; 22. For Mars, it is 10; 8; 8; 26; 16. For Mercury, being in an enemy's house, one-third is deducted, leaving 6; 0; 3; 34; 4. For Jupiter, it is 10; 11; 27; 28; but because it is in the eighth house, one-tenth is deducted, resulting in 9; 10; 21; 43; 30. For Venus, it is 16; 7; 16; 17; 2; but being in the twelfth house and an enemy's house, it is halved and then a third is deducted, resulting in 5; 5; 16; 25; 4. For Saturn, it is 8; 11; 14; 55; 14. For the Ascendant <term>Lagna: the rising sign</term>, the longevity by degrees is 6; 4; 26; 22; 12. This constitutes the longevity of the birth chart according to the opinion of Jeevasharma. (6)

### Now, following this same explanation, the Teacher <note>referring to Varahamihira</note> describes the calculation of longevity in an Arya verse:

# In the method of Satya, convert the desired planet into minutes and divide by two hundred.
# The years are what remain after removing multiples of twelve; from the remainder, months etc. are found. (10)

"In the method of Satya" means in the calculation of longevity according to the school of Satyacharya. One should take the "desired planet" <note>its longitudinal position</note> at the time of birth, convert it into minutes <term>lipta: minutes of arc</term> to create a total sum of minutes, and divide that by two hundred. The quotient obtained should be set aside. The remainder should be placed below. From the quotient, "years are what remain after removing multiples of twelve." By the term "multiples of twelve" <term>mandalabhaga</term>, the twelve signs are meant; therefore, divide the quotient by twelve and discard the multiples of twelve. Whatever remains are the years—that is how many years of life are given by that planet. "From the remainder, months etc.": from the remainder that was set aside, multiplied by twelve and divided by that same divisor <note>200</note>, the months are obtained. From that remainder multiplied by thirty, the days. From that remainder multiplied by sixty, the ghatikas <note>units of 24 minutes</note>. Again, by multiplying by sixty and dividing as before, the seconds <term>vikalas</term> are obtained. The result thus arrived at is the longevity contribution of the planet.

---

<note>Logic here: According to the saying "The truth-telling words (of Satya) achieve great consistency by being equal to the signs and Navamshas traversed by the planet," a planet situated in the first Navamsha <term>one-ninth of a sign</term> of Aries gives one year of life. In the second Navamsha (Taurus), two years. In the third (Gemini), three years... and so on, up to the twelfth Navamsha (Pisces), which gives twelve years. To find the Navamsha of a planet, the ratio is: if 200 minutes equals one Navamsha, then how many Navamshas do the minutes of the desired planet equal?</note>

Planet X 1
----------
   200
</margin>

In this calculation, since anything beyond twelve years is not required <note>as the cycle repeats every 12 signs</note>, one should divide by twelve and the remainder is the year-measure. Likewise, from the remainder of the division by two hundred, the months etc. should be calculated. For example, multiply the year-remainder by twelve and divide by the divisor to get the months. Multiply the month-remainder by thirty and divide by the divisor to get the days. Multiply the day-remainder by sixty and divide by the divisor to get the ghatikas. In this way, the palam <note>smaller time units</note> are also calculated. Thus $\therefore$ it is proven.

Here is an example: The position of the planet at the time of birth is 1 Sign, 8 Degrees, 45 Minutes, 0 Seconds. When converted entirely into minutes <note>original: "liptā-piṇḍīkṛtaḥ"</note>, it becomes 2325. Dividing this by two hundred (200), the quotient obtained is 11 and the remainder is 125. Since this quotient of 11 cannot be divided further by twelve, this remains the value. Therefore, eleven years are given by this planet. The remainder of 125 is multiplied by twelve, resulting in 1500. Dividing this by two hundred, the quotient is 7; thus, seven months. Then, the remaining 100 from the months is multiplied by thirty (30), resulting in 3000. Dividing this by two hundred, the quotient is 15; thus, fifteen days. Since there is no further remainder, there are no *ghatikas* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. Thus, the years and other units derived from such a planet are: 11 Years, 7 Months, 15 Days, 0 Ghatikas.

Now, the same is demonstrated by the rule of multiplying the signs, degrees, and minutes. It is as follows: The planet in signs etc. is 1 | 8 | 45. The signs, degrees, and minutes are each multiplied by twelve: 12 | 96 | 540. Then, these are further multiplied by nine: 108 | 864 | 4860. Here, dividing these 4860 minutes by sixty, the quotient is 81 and the remainder is 0. This quotient, representing *ghatikas*, is added to the degrees (864), totaling 945. Dividing this by thirty, the quotient is 31 and the remainder is 15; these are the days. Now, adding this quotient of 31 to the signs (108), the total is 139. Dividing this by twelve, the quotient is 11 and the remainder is 7; these are the months. Since the quotient 11 cannot be divided by twelve, it remains as the remainder 11. These are the years of life granted by the planet: 11 Years, 7 Months, 15 Days, 0 Ghatikas. This matches the previously calculated lifespan. Thus has the lifespan been shown by Yavanesvara, Satyacharya, Badarayana, and Varahamihira. 10

**Vernacular Explanation**—According to the opinion of Satyacharya, convert every planet's position into minutes <note>original: "kalātmaka"</note> and divide by 200. From the remaining minutes, calculate the months and other units. In this way, the <term>Ayurdaya</term> <note>The span of life or longevity contributed by a celestial body</note> of that planet in years etc. is determined. 10

The mathematical proof (logic) for this is that the minutes in 1 Sign are 1800; one-ninth of that (a Navamsha) is 200 minutes. From this, the proportion is: if 200 minutes equal 1 Navamsha, then how many are in the desired planet's minutes? Thus:
Elapsed Navamshas = <u>Planet in minutes</u> / 200
If the number of Navamshas is greater than 12, it should be reduced by multiples of 12 <note>original: "taṣṭita"</note>, because an elapsed Navamsha is equivalent to a year. There are only 12 signs. From the remaining minutes, the proportion is: if 200 minutes equal 12 months, then what do the remaining minutes equal? In this way, by multiplying the remaining minutes by 12 and dividing by 200, the quotient is months; further...

Now, using the *Vanshastha* meter, he describes the specific adjustments to the longevity calculated according to the school of Satyacharya:

->**The years given by a planet are tripled if it is in its exaltation or in retrograde motion. They are doubled if the planet is in its "best division" (Vargottama), its own Navamsha, its own sign, or its own Decan (Drekkana). This is the specific distinction taught by Bhadatta (Satyacharya); other rules remain the same as previously stated.**<- ||11||

**Commentary:** *In its exaltation or retrograde:* For planets situated in their highest point of exaltation or moving in retrograde motion, the longevity they grant should be multiplied by three. *Doubled:* For those in the *Vargottama* <note>the best ninth-part division where a planet occupies the same sign in both the main chart and the ninth-part chart</note>, or in their own *Navamsha* <note>ninth-part division</note>, or in their own zodiac sign, or in their own *Drekkana* <note>ten-degree division or Decan</note>, the longevity granted must be multiplied by two. *This specific distinction:* The word "Bhadatta" refers to the teacher Satyacharya, whose authority is being established here. Previously, longevity was calculated according to the methods of Maya, Yavana, Manittha, and others. The distinction in Satyacharya’s teaching is this specific tripling and doubling. *Other rules remain the same:* The remaining rules are the same as those mentioned in the first method (the school of Maya and Yavana). This means: after calculating longevity by Satyacharya’s method, one must still subtract one-third for a planet in an enemy’s house (except for retrograde planets) and subtract half for a planet that is combust <note>hidden by the sun's light</note>, except for Venus and Saturn. Reductions for planets in the visible hemisphere (Chakra-pata) must also be performed as previously described. ||11||

**Vernacular Translation**—Having calculated the longevity according to Satyacharya’s view, if a planet is in its exaltation or is retrograde, its contribution to longevity should be tripled. If it is in its *Vargottama Navamsha* or its own *Drekkana*, its contribution should be doubled. This process is the unique feature of Satyacharya’s method compared to other teachers. All other procedures (subtracting one-third for being in an enemy's house, subtracting half for being combust, and the reductions for the half-zodiac) are the same; that is, they should be understood as identical in Bhadatta’s (Satyacharya’s) system. ||11||

-> **Sanskrit Commentary by Bhattotpala with Hindi Translation** <-

The number of years corresponding to the portion of the <term>Lagna</term><note>The Ascendant or the rising sign at the time of birth.</note> already traversed constitutes the <term>Lagna-Ayurdaya</term><note>Longevity contributed specifically by the Ascendant.</note>. For the remaining portions consisting of degrees and minutes, the months and days should be calculated using the <term>Rule of Three</term><note>A mathematical method (proportion) to find a fourth value knowing three others.</note>. This is what is meant: according to the teachings of Satyacharya, the <term>Lagna-Ayurdaya</term> should be calculated by converting the desired portion of the sign into minutes. 

If the <term>Hora</term><note>The Ascendant/Lagna.</note> is endowed with strength—meaning it is occupied or aspected by its own lord, Jupiter, or Mercury, and not by others—then it grants years equal to the number of signs passed. As the rule states: *"If the Hora is aspected or joined by its lord, Jupiter, or Mercury, and not by others,"* then a powerful Ascendant gives years equal to the signs. 

How are the months and days calculated from the degrees and minutes via the <term>Rule of Three</term>? The degrees and minutes are collected into a single sum of minutes, multiplied by twelve, and divided by eighteen hundred; the quotient gives the months. The remainder is multiplied by thirty and divided by the same divisor to get the days. That remainder is multiplied by sixty to get the <term>Ghatikas</term><note>A traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note>, and the next remainder by sixty for the <term>Chashakas</term><note>A smaller unit of time, roughly 24 seconds.</note>. The resulting months and days are added to the total; thus is the <term>Lagna-Ayurdaya</term> determined. 

What is prescribed for a strong Ascendant must not be applied to one devoid of strength. On this, **Badarayana** says: *"The longevity of the Hora is likewise; if strong, it grants years equal to the signs; the results for the remaining degrees are found by proportion."* This was also stated without contradiction by **Varahamihira** in his *Svalpa Jataka*. 

Regarding the "Rising of a Malefic": In the systems of Maya, Yavana, and others, when a malefic planet is in the Ascendant, a reduction is made according to the rule *"multiplied by the portion of the Navamsha risen."* However, in this system of Satyacharya, such a reduction should **not** be performed; all other procedures remain. Furthermore, one should not use the years previously taught—the ninety-nine years mentioned in the systems of Yavana and Badarayana, or the maximum lifespan fractions of Jivasharma. The <term>Rule of Three</term> based on those years does not apply here. For example, if the Sun's nineteen years correspond to twelve <term>Navamshas</term><note>A 1/9th division of a zodiac sign.</note>, one should not calculate what a single <term>Navamsha</term> gives based on that ratio when following Satyacharya's method. || 12 ||

**Hindi Translation —** According to the opinion of **Satyacharya**, the longevity consists of as many years as there are <term>Navamshas</term> traversed in the Ascendant. However, if the Ascendant is strong—meaning it is aspected by or joined with its lord, Mercury, or Jupiter—it grants additional years equal to the signs traversed. Furthermore, the reduction (loss of years) prescribed by other teachers (such as Maya) when a malefic planet is in the Ascendant is **not** to be applied in Satyacharya's method. Additionally, the <term>Lagna-Ayurdaya</term> should not be calculated using the years previously mentioned (such as the 120-year cycle or the seventh-part divisions of the <term>Paramayurdaya</term><note>The maximum theoretical lifespan.</note>). This is the specific distinction in Satyacharya's school compared to other teachers. || 12 ||

**Example—** Taking the previously recorded longitude of the Sun at 0 signs, 6 degrees, 46 minutes, and 40 seconds: converting this into minutes gives 406 minutes and 40 seconds. Dividing this by 200 <note>The divisor 200 relates to the mathematical conversion of planetary arcs into years of life in this specific system</note>, the quotient is 2. Since this is less than twelve, the years contributed by the Sun are 2. Multiplying the remainder 6;40 by 12 gives 116;0; dividing this by 200 gives a quotient of 0 months. Then, multiplying the remainder 116 by 30 and dividing by 200 gives 17 days. Finally, multiplying the remaining 80 by 60 and dividing by 200 gives 24 *ghatis* <term>Ghati: a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term>. Thus, the Sun’s contribution to the lifespan is 2 years, 0 months, 17 days, and 24 ghatis.

Similarly, because the Moon is "combust" <note>original: 'astangata'; rendered powerless by being too close to the Sun</note>, its value of 3;8;4;42;36 is halved to 1;10;2;21;18. Mars contributes 10;0;0;48;36. For Mercury, after subtracting one-third <note>original: 'vyanshon'; a reduction applied due to specific planetary debilities</note>, the value is 6;10;8;54;0. For Jupiter, after subtracting one-tenth, it is 6;6;6;43;45. For Venus, because it is in the twelfth house, its initial value of 7;10;24;12;36 is halved to 3;11;12;6;18; then, because it is in an enemy's sign, another third is subtracted to get 2;7;18;4;12. However, since Venus is in its sign of exaltation <note>original: 'svoccha'</note>, this value is tripled, resulting in a final corrected value for Venus of 7;10;24;12;36. Saturn contributes 8;5;4;36;0 and the Ascendant <term>Lagna: the rising sign at the moment of birth</term> contributes 6;4;26;22;12. 

Jupiter is in the *Vargottama Navamsha* <note>A highly auspicious position where the planet occupies the same sign in both the main birth chart and the 1/9th divisional chart; here, Scorpio</note>, therefore its lifespan contribution is doubled to 13;0;16;27;30. The Sun is in its exaltation, so its calculated value is tripled to 6;1;12;12. Thus, according to the school of Satyacharya, the total sum of the lifespan contributions from the planets and the Ascendant for this birth is 62 years, 5 months, 21 days, 18 ghatis, and 30 palas.

A simpler method for calculating this lifespan contribution is as follows: If 12 signs contain 108 *Navamshas* <note>1/9th divisions of a sign</note>, then how many are in the planet's traveled longitude?

Using the Rule of Three <term>Trairashika: a mathematical proportion</term>: 
Number of Navamshas = $\frac{\text{Planet's Longitude} \times 108}{12}$

From this, it is proven that by multiplying the planet's longitude by 108 and converting the seconds, then dividing the sign position by 12, the quotient equals the years. If the quotient exceeds 12, divide by 12 and take the remainder as the years; the remaining fractions should be understood as months, days, etc. The Author (Varahamihira) has stated this same method in his shorter work, the *Laghu Jataka*:

> "The signs, degrees, and minutes of a planet, multiplied by twelve and nine, and divided by the full circle; the resulting cycles are discarded, and the remainder gives the years, months, and so on." <note>original: 'Rāśyaṃśakalā guṇitā...'</note> This has a clear meaning.

->Now, having presented the opinions of Maya and others, and the opinion of Jivasharma, he states the acceptance of Satyacharya’s opinion in the Indravajra meter:<-

# The teaching of Satya is best here, but they make it unfit through many multiplications.
# The rule of the teachers regarding multiple multipliers is that only the one which is the greatest should be applied. || 13 ||

**The teaching of Satya...** In these three schools of thought, the teaching of Satyacharya is the best or most excellent. However, in the end, they make it "unfit" or destroy its accuracy through "many multiplications" (calculations). What are these calculations? They are rules such as "triple the value for a planet in its exaltation or retrograde motion," and so on. In that system, if a planet is in its own house, they double the lifespan. If that same planet is in its own subdivision (Navamsha), they double it again. If it is in its own <term>decanate</term> <note>original: "drekkana"; a 10-degree solar division</note>, they double it yet again. If it is in the <term>best subdivision</term> <note>original: "vargottama"; where a planet occupies the same sign in both the main chart and the 9th harmonic chart</note> and is also <term>retrograde</term> <note>original: "vakri"</note>, they triple it again. If it is in its exaltation, they triple it again. Thus, there is no finality (anavastha). Due to this risk of infinite regression, they make the lifespan calculated by Satya improper through these many multiplications. As Maya says:

> "In the best subdivision, in one's own sign, in one's decanate, or in one's own ninth-part, it is double. In retrograde or exaltation, it is triple; the doubling is applied respectively."

And so it is said in the **Saravali**:

> "Regarding the attainment of many multiplications, the single multiplication which the teacher Varahamihira performs was not seen by the ancients."

This has also been stated. So, what should be done here? He says: **"The rule of the teachers regarding multiple multipliers."** This "rule of the teachers" refers to the traditional doctrine (Agama). When multiple multiplications are applicable, "only the one which is the greatest" calculation should be performed. Among many potential calculations, only one is done. Where doubling is required multiple times, the lifespan should be doubled only once. Where both doubling and tripling are required, it should be tripled only once. Where tripling is required twice, it should be tripled only once. This is because of the statement: **"Only the one which is the greatest should be applied."** As in the Svalpa Jataka—

The Teacher <note>referring to Varahamihira, the author</note> has also stated:
> 'In the **Vargottama** <term>Vargottama: a planet occupying the same sign in both the main birth chart and the ninth divisional chart, increasing its strength</term>, in its own **Decan** <term>Drekkana: a 10-degree solar division</term>, or in its own **Ninth-part** <term>Navamsha: a 3.25-degree solar division</term>, the years are doubled once. For a planet in **Retrograde** or in **Exaltation** <term>the sign where a planet is strongest</term>, they are tripled; if multiple conditions for doubling or tripling are met, the tripling is applied only once.'</note>

Excluding the reduction for the "descent of the wheel" <note>Chakra-pata: a specific calculation based on a planet's position in the visible or invisible hemisphere</note>, according to the rule of multiple multiplications, if a planet is in an enemy’s sign, in its sign of **Debilitation** <term>Neecha: the sign where a planet is weakest</term>, or **Combust** <term>hidden by the Sun's rays</term>, then a reduction must be made only once. The rule "the debilitated planet loses half" should also be followed here. It is said in the *Svalpa Jataka*:
> 'Planets in an enemy’s sign lose one-third; in debilitation, they lose half; and those whose rays are obscured by the Sun also lose half. However, Saturn and Venus do not lose their strength when combust.'</note>

By doing this, the clarity of Sage Satyacharya’s opinion is established; this is the Teacher's view. Where a reduction is required, one should perform the reduction only once and the multiplication only once. However, when a reduction is to be made, one should first perform the "descent of the wheel" reduction, then the reduction for being in an enemy’s sign only once, and then the multiplication only once.

On this matter, the venerable **Garga** says:
> 'A planet grants years equal to the number of degrees it has traversed in a sign. The **Ascendant** <term>Lagna: the sign rising on the eastern horizon at birth</term>, if strong, grants years equal to the number of signs it has passed. The calculation of months and days should be done by proportion. Malefic planets in the 12th, 11th, 10th, 9th, and 8th houses from the Ascendant take away all, a half, a third, a fourth, or a sixth of the lifespan respectively; other planets <note>benefics</note> take away half of that. This is known as the "descent of the wheel" reduction. If many planets are in one sign, only the strongest one causes the reduction. A planet in an enemy’s sign loses a third; one in debilitation or combust loses half. Saturn, Venus, and Mars do not lose their portion when in an enemy’s sign. When multiple reductions are applicable, only the greatest one should be performed. Similarly, only the single greatest multiplication should be applied: by two if in Vargottama, its own Ninth-part, its own Decan, or its own sign; by three if Retrograde or in its sign of Exaltation. This is how the lifespan is determined after subtractions and additions.'</note>

Although the Teacher has authorized the **Amsayu** <term>lifespan calculated by degrees</term> method, it should be used only if the Ascendant is fully strong. If the Sun is stronger, then **Pindayu** <term>lifespan calculated by planetary totals</term> should be used. As **Manittha** says:
> 'When the Ascendant is endowed with great strength and aspected by benefics, the degree-based lifespan occurs. The ancients say that if the Sun is stronger, one should use the total-based lifespan.'</note>

And so it is in the *Saravali*:
> 'Lifespan from the Ascendant is degree-based; from the Sun, it is total-based; and from the Moon, it is natural-based.'</note>

Others say this: both the degree-based and total-based lifespans should be calculated, and the division of major and sub-periods <note>Dashas and Antardashas</note> should be projected from both. If the shorter lifespan's final sub-period coincides with the longer one's current period, the person lives the longer life. If it is the period of an enemy planet, death occurs then; if a friend's period, they live; if a neutral period, they suffer but survive. We favor the opinion of Sage Satyacharya. || 13 ||

People perform many calculations (following the rules such as "attained through exaltation or retrograde motion," etc.) and end up making them improper or incorrect. True mastery (scholarship) consists of this: if multiple multipliers are applicable, the largest calculation should be chosen and applied only once. || 13 ||

**Special Meaning—** The intention is that according to the opinion of the True Teacher <note>Satyacharya, a respected authority in astrology</note>, when calculating the lifespan, if a planet is both retrograde and in its exaltation, people often triple the lifespan twice. That is improper. In that case, one should triple it only once. Similarly, where both doubling and tripling are applicable, one should only triple. And where both a reduction of one-third and a reduction of one-half are applicable, one should only reduce by half; not both. This is the opinion of Varahamihira. || 13 ||

Now, in the *Pushpitagra* meter, he describes a combination (Yoga) where the measure of life for one born under it cannot be calculated:

->**When Jupiter and the Moon are in Cancer as the Ascendant, and Mercury and Venus are in the Cardinal houses (Kendras), while the remaining planets are in the eleventh, sixth, and third houses, the lifespan here is infinite, without the need for sequential calculation.** || 14<-

Thus ends the Seventh Chapter on Lifespan (Ayurdaya) in the *Brihat Jataka* composed by the Great Teacher Varahamihira. (1) || 7 ||

**Commentary:** Regarding "Jupiter etc."—When there is a Cancer Ascendant (the sign of the Crab) with Jupiter and the Moon residing there, and Mercury and Venus are in the *Kendras* (the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses), and the remaining planets—the Sun, Mars, and Saturn—are in the 11th (house of gains), 6th (house of enemies), or 3rd (house of siblings); in such a combination, the life of the person born is infinite or immeasurable, even without the sequential mathematical operations. This is what is said: when Cancer is the Ascendant and the Moon and Jupiter are situated right there, and Mercury and Venus are together or separate in any of the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses as possible, and the remaining Sun, Mars, and Saturn are together or separate in the 11th, 6th, or 3rd houses, then the person born in such a combination has a lifespan of immeasurable proportions. This meaning applies even without the results derived from standard mathematics.

# Page 178
### Chapter on Longevity from the Brihat Jataka

In such a planetary combination <note>original: "yoga"</note>, the calculation of longevity should not be performed because it is considered impossible to limit. Therefore, for a person born under different circumstances, the lifespan must be determined as it comes. Death does not occur before the calculated sum of years, nor can one live beyond that sum. In certain combinations, the life of an immoral person is destroyed. As stated in the sacred law <note>original: "Smriti"</note>: "Adultery shortens life," and through such vices, one does not survive. However, a person born under this specific combination who uses life-prolonging elixirs <note>term: Rasayanas; alchemical or herbal tonics used in Ayurveda for rejuvenation</note> according to the prescribed methods of Ayurveda attains a very long life. ||14||

->Thus ends the seventh chapter on Longevity in the commentary on Brihat Jataka composed by Shri Bhattotpala.<-

**Vernacular—** If the Ascendant <note>term: Lagna; the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at birth</note> is Cancer containing both the Moon and Jupiter, while Mercury and Venus are in the center houses <note>term: Kendra; the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</note>, and the remaining planets (Saturn, Sun, Mars) are in the 11th, 6th, or 3rd houses from the Ascendant—either together or separately—then one should disregard the standard mathematical sequence and consider that person's lifespan to be beyond measure. ||14||

**Special Meaning—** The intent is that a person born in such a favorable combination performs good deeds, and therefore their lifespan increases. This also proves that a person born in the opposite combination is engaged in evil deeds (a sinner), which leads to the loss of life. It is said: "From virtuous conduct comes the increase of life, and from sinful conduct comes its certain destruction." ||14||

Thus, from the beginning of the first quarter to the beginning of the second quarter, a reduction equal to one-sixth of the maximum lifespan is observed. The same reduction applies from the second to the third, and from the third to the fourth. Since the reduction is exactly one-sixth of the maximum life, the desired lifespan should be calculated by proportion based on the elapsed time of the birth star <note>term: Bhayata; the time elapsed since the Moon entered the current Nakshatra</note>. Taking the total duration of the star as a rough measure of 60 units, the proportion is: if a 15-ghati <note>note: a ghati is a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> duration of elapsed star-time results in a reduction of one-sixth of the maximum life, then how much reduction results from the desired elapsed star-time?

| 120 x Elapsed Time | | 120 x Elapsed Time | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| ------------------ | = | ------------------ | = | Resulting Reduction |
| 6 x 15 | | 90 | | |

Subtracting this from the maximum lifespan gives the remaining clear desired lifespan. As stated in the verses of the *Gauri Jataka*:

> "Multiply the elapsed minutes of the birth star by the maximum lifespan. 
> Divide by ninety and subtract that portion from the maximum lifespan of the man; 
> the remainder shall be the clear lifespan. 
> From this proportion, the planetary periods <note>term: Dashas; planetary cycles that rule specific periods of a person's life</note> should also be calculated."

**Meaning of this:—** The calculator should multiply the elapsed minutes of the birth star <note>original: "Nakshatra"</note> by the maximum lifespan (120 years). Divide that by ninety. Subtract the quotient obtained from the maximum lifespan (120 years). The remainder is the clear lifespan of the man. Furthermore, the planetary periods <note>Dashas</note> should be calculated by the mathematician based on this proportion.

**Example here:—** At someone's birth, the elapsed star-time <note>Bhayata-ghati</note> is 20:15. Then, according to the verse above: the maximum lifespan = 120, multiplied by the elapsed time = 2400 : 1800. When converted, it becomes 2430:0. Divided by ninety, the resulting years are 27. Subtracting this from the maximum lifespan: 120 - 27 = 93 years, which is the desired measure of the lifespan.

# Chapter 8: On Major and Minor Planetary Periods

Now, the chapter on Major Periods <note>Dasha</note> and Minor Periods <note>Antardasha</note> is explained. For a person whose total lifespan has been determined, the division of happiness and distress occurring within that life is now established. In this system, the duration of the period belonging to a specific planet is exactly equal to the lifespan contributed by that planet after the necessary mathematical adjustments <note>shodhya-kshepa-vishuddham</note>. However, the sequence of these periods is not immediately known; to provide that knowledge, the author speaks in the **Malini** meter:

## Those situated in the Ascendant, Sun, or Moon—whichever is strongest—and those in the Centers and following houses,
## Give their results in the first, middle, and final stages of life.
## It is not that the ripening of results does not occur if planets are absent from the Centers;
## For the ripening of fruit occurs even in the Cadent houses first [if others are empty]. || 1 ||

**Commentary:** Regarding "Those situated in...": The **Ascendant** <note>Udaya</note> represents the body; the **Sun** <note>Ravi</note> represents the soul; the **Moon** <note>Shashanka</note> represents the mind. Among these three—the Ascendant, the Sun, and the Moon—the first major period belongs to whichever is the strongest <note>prani</note>, because of its primary importance to embodied beings. As **Yavaneshvara** <note>An early authority on Indian astrology, often linked to Greco-Indian transmissions</note> says:
> "Among the Moon, the Sun, and the Ascendant, whichever possesses the greatest strength through the planetary combinations of that time, its period is declared first; the others follow in order of their remaining strength."

The first period is granted by the strongest of the Ascendant, Sun, or Moon. Following that, the planets situated in the **Centers, Succedent, and Cadent houses** <term>Kendra, Panaphara, Apoklima</term> <note>These terms correspond to the 1st/4th/7th/10th houses, 2nd/5th/8th/11th, and 3rd/6th/9th/12th respectively</note> give their periods in order of their increasing or decreasing strength. Thus, one must first determine the period of the strongest among the Ascendant, Sun, and Moon. Then, the periods of the planets situated in the Centers relative to that strongest point are arranged. Those in the Centers give their results in the first stage of life. As it was said: "They give results in the first, middle, and final stages." **Yavaneshvara** also states:
> "Planets in the Centers bear fruit in the first part of life; those in Succedent houses in the middle age; and those in Cadent houses give fruit at the end of life. Whichever is strongest among them comes first."

Now, if there are no planets in the Centers, who gives the fruit in the first stage of life? The author says: "It is not that the ripening of results does not occur," etc. In the absence of planets in the Centers, it is not that there is no ripening of results in the first stage of life. The two negatives <note>double negative</note> emphasize the intended meaning. If planets are also absent from Succedent houses, it is not that there is no ripening in middle age. If absent from Cadent houses, it is not that there is no ripening in the final stage. This means: when there are no planets in the Centers, those in the Succedent houses provide the early results, followed by those in the Cadent houses. If both Centers and Succedent houses are empty, then the planets in the Cadent houses provide the results throughout the entire life.

# Chapter on Planetary Periods and Sub-periods

<page-num>180</page-num>
->The Great Compendium of Nativity<-

...yields results. As it has been stated: "The ripening of fruits occurs even in the <term>Apoklima</term><note>The 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th houses, considered the weakest positions</note> houses earlier." Thus, in the absence of planets in the Apoklima houses, those in the <term>Kendras</term><note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses; the pillars of the horoscope</note> yield results first, followed by those in the <term>Panapharas</term><note>The 2nd, 5th, 8th, and 11th houses; succedent houses</note>. When there are no planets in the Apoklima or Panaphara houses, then the planets in the Kendras yield results throughout the entire lifespan. 

This is what is meant: "Whichever among the Ascendant, the Sun, and the Moon is strongest, their period shall be the first." After determining the first period, the periods of all planets situated in the Kendras relative to that first ruler should be arranged. After those are arranged, the periods of those in the Panapharas should be set, followed by those in the Apoklimas. In the absence of planets in the Kendras, the periods of those in the Panapharas follow the first ruler, then the Apoklimas. If both Kendras and Panapharas are empty, only the Apoklimas are arranged. If there are planets in Kendras and Apoklimas but not in Panapharas, then after the Kendras, the Apoklimas follow. If only Kendras are occupied, only they are arranged; if only Panapharas, then only they; if only Apoklimas, then only they. 

As stated in the *Svalpa Jataka*:

> "Whichever among the Ascendant, the Sun, and the Moon is strongest, its period is first.
> The remaining periods follow based on the strength of those in the Kendras, Panapharas, and Apoklimas." || 1 ||

**Vernacular Commentary**—Among the Ascendant (<term>Lagna</term>), the Sun (<term>Ravi</term>), and the Moon (<term>Chandra</term>), whichever is the most powerful has the first period at the start of life. Then follow the periods of planets in the Kendra positions relative to it. After that, in the middle of life, come the periods of planets in the Panaphara positions. Finally, at the end of life, come the periods of planets in the Apoklima positions. If there are no planets in the Kendras or Panapharas, one should not think "there will be no results in the first or middle age"; rather, in that case, the periods of planets in the Apoklima (3, 6, 9, 12) positions will cover those times. || 1 ||

Now, the author explains the duration of the periods and the sequence of periods for planets within the Kendras using the <term>Indravajra</term><note>A specific Sanskrit poetic meter</note> verse:

**The lifespan contributed by a planet is its period; the strongest planet's period comes first. If strengths are equal, the one providing more years comes first; if those are also equal, the one that rose first in the sky takes precedence.** || 2 ||

**Commentary on "The lifespan contributed":** The number of years of life granted by a planet—after necessary mathematical reductions and additions—is to be considered that planet's period (<term>Dasha</term>). Following the rule that the strongest among the Ascendant, Sun, and Moon starts first, one determines the first period. Then, among the planets in the Kendras, the period of the one with the greatest strength is placed first. Afterward, the periods of those with less strength are arranged in descending order. After arranging the periods of those in the Kendras...

<header>Including the Hindi commentary and the Sanskrit commentary by Bhattotpala</header>

Of those in the <term>Panaphara</term><note>Succedent houses: the 2nd, 5th, 8th, and 11th houses</note> positions. The sequence for those in the Panaphara positions should be determined in this same manner. Then, the sequence for those in the <term>Apoklima</term><note>Cadent houses: the 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th houses</note> positions follows the same rule. Regarding the phrase "when many are equal": if many planets in the <term>Kendra</term><note>Angular houses: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</note> positions have equal strength, the first <term>Dasha</term><note>Planetary period or life-stage</note> is assigned to the one who grants the most years. Now, one might ask: how can planets have exactly equal strength? If two planets are both in a friendly sign, their own trine, or their exaltation, then the one with the greater natural strength would be considered stronger. That may be so; however, when the strengths of position, direction, motion, time, and planetary aspects are mathematically combined, an equality of strength can occur. For a general example: if Saturn is joined with three units of strength and Mars with two, then because of Mars's inherent natural strength, their total strength becomes equal. This should be understood for all planets. And if their strength is equal, the rule is "of the one who rose first." Even if the number of years granted is equal, the Dasha of the one who rose first must be arranged. Among those who have risen or emerged from the solar disc, when strength is equal, the Dasha of the one with greater strength is arranged first, even if another grants more years. Regarding "the one who rose first" in cases of equal strength, there are two types of rising: one due to the daily rotation of the zodiac, and the other due to separation from the Sun. In this context, "rising" refers to the separation from the Sun, which is known through the degrees of time mentioned in the mathematical branch of astronomy.

On this subject, the Lord Garga says:

> "The strongest among the Ascendant, the Moon, and the Sun grants the first period.
> After that, the planets in the Angular, Succedent, and Cadent houses grant theirs in sequence.
> Among those, the stronger one comes first; if strength is equal, the one who gives more years.
> If those are also equal, the period is given by the one who first emerged from the Sun." ||2||

**Vernacular Language** — According to the previous rule, the lifespan (years, etc.) contributed by a planet should be understood as that planet's Dasha period. That Dasha also follows the order of strength; that is, the strongest planet's Dasha occurs first. If two or more planets are equal in strength, the Dasha of the one who has more years should be considered first. If the years are also equal, the Dasha of the one who first rose after being combust <note>original: "asta"</note> due to proximity to the Sun occurs first. ||2||

**Special Meaning** — It is stated here that if strength and years are equal, the Dasha of the one who rose first after solar proximity should be considered first. But if there is equality even in the rising after solar proximity, then whose Dasha will come first? A decision on this has not been stated here. Therefore, the decision mentioned by Nilakantha should be applied: "the one with the slower motion comes first" <note>original: "alpagatestu purva"</note>. This means the planet whose orbit is higher <note>further from Earth</note> has its Dasha first, because there can be no equality in the planetary orbits. ||2||

## Chapter on Planetary Periods and Sub-periods in the Brihat Jataka

The method for calculation was previously demonstrated. For the sake of clarity, here is the table for the *Anshayurdaya* <note>A system of longevity calculation based on the degrees of planetary positions</note> cycle:

| Period Lord | Sun | Moon | Ascendant | Saturn | Jupiter | Venus | Mars | Mercury |

| | 6 | 3 | 6 | 8 | 13 | 7 | 10 | 6 |

->A planet in the same sign takes half;<-
->one in a trine house takes a third; one in the seventh takes a seventh part;<-
->and one in a square house takes a fourth part of the fruit. Together with the Ascendant,<-

**A planet in the same sign takes half:** This means a planet situated in the same zodiac sign as the Period Lord <term>Dashapati: the planet currently ruling the major life cycle</term> takes half of the sub-period time allotted by that Lord and matures it according to its own planetary qualities. 

**One in a trine house takes a third:** A planet located in a trine <note>The 5th or 9th house positions</note> from the Period Lord takes one-third of the sub-period time and matures it through its own qualities. 

**One in the seventh takes a seventh part:** A planet situated in the seventh house <note>directly opposite</note> from the Period Lord takes a seventh part of the sub-period time and matures it. 

**One in a square house takes a fourth:** A planet situated in the fourth or eighth houses <note>known here as the 'square' or Chaturasra positions</note> from the Period Lord takes a fourth part of the sub-period time and matures it. 

**Together with the Ascendant:** The Ascendant <term>Hora: the rising sign or Lagna</term> is included in this calculation. All these, arranged in this manner relative to one another, mature the results according to their respective planetary strengths. 

The meaning is this: just as a planet situated in the same sign (or other positions) as the Period Lord matures its assigned portion, the Ascendant also matures a portion. In this calculation, one must first determine the portion of the Period Lord, and then calculate the portions for the planets situated in the same sign, etc. Because the half-shares and other fractions for the remaining planets are derived based on the portion that comes from the Period Lord.

# Page 183
### Commentary by Bhattotpala with Hindi Translation

Now, when many planets are situated in a single house, among them, only the one who is the strongest <note>the planet with the highest Shadbala or positional strength</note> brings about the ripening <note>term: ripening (pachayati); refers to the planet acting as the ruler of a sub-period or Antardasha</note> of results; the others do not. How is this known? It is said: because of the use of the singular number in the instructions. As it is stated:
> "A planet **occupying the same sign** gives away half of its own [period]."
In this and other passages, the singular number is used. Not only did the teacher Mihira <note>Varahamihira, the 6th-century author of the Brihat Jataka</note> use the singular, but it is also stated as such in the *Svalpa Jataka*:
> "A planet situated in the **same sign** ripens half; in the **two trines** (5th and 9th), a third part; in the **seventh**, a seventh part; and in the **two squares** (4th and 8th), a fourth part, according to its own qualities."
Furthermore, the use of the singular is also found in the works of Garga and others. Thus, the Sage Garga says:
> "One staying in the **same sign** [takes] half; one in a **trine**, a third part; one in the **seventh**, a seventh part; and one in the **fourth or eighth**, a fourth part. All these, including the Ascendant, bestow results upon one another."
Yavanesvara <note>The "Lord of the Greeks," an early authority on Indian astrology</note> also says the same:
> "The time for one residing in the **same house** is a half-share; in the **fourth**, it receives half of that (a fourth); in a **trine**, it is a sharer of a third; and in the **seventh**, the planet becomes a sharer of a seventh part according to its movement."
Thus, the singular is used everywhere. From this, it is understood that only one planet becomes the "divider of parts" <note>term: amshaharo; the one who reduces or claims a portion of the years</note>, not all of them. Satyacharya says the same:
> "Half, a third, half of a half (a fourth), and a seventh part. For those in the **same sign, ninth, fifth, fourth, eighth, and seventh**... planets give these to the planets known as sub-period lords in their own major periods. In the case of those in the same sign, the **strongest** is the divider of parts, whether a friend or an enemy. If a friend, the result is robust; at that time, an enemy is not so."
And Yama says:
> "Among those who have reached the **same sign**, he who is specifically the **strongest** is the sole taker; the other birds <note>metaphor for planets</note> situated there are not."
Even regarding the Ascendant (Lagna), where the taking of parts is applicable, if a planet is situated in the Ascendant, then between the Ascendant and the planet, whichever is **stronger** alone takes the prescribed part, not the other. Others, however, desire a sub-period share for all planets occupying the same sign. Still others, taking only one share, divide that share among all planets in the same sign. || 3 ||

---

**Vernacular Translation:**
(The lord of the major period is the master of the total lifespan, therefore his share is complete.) Among the planets staying with the major period lord, only the **single strongest planet** becomes the ripener (sub-period lord) of one-half (1/2). Similarly, among those in the trines (9th and 5th), one strong planet becomes the sub-period lord of one-third (1/3). One planet in the seventh house from the major period lord ripens a seventh part (1/7). And among planets in the square (4th and 8th) positions, only one strong planet ripens a fourth part (1/4). In this way, all planets, including the Ascendant, falling in these positions relative to each other, give results as sub-period lords according to their respective qualities. || 3 ||

**Special Meaning:**
Here, the interpretation that only one planet among those in the same sign or trines etc., becomes the "ripener" is derived from the use of the **singular number** in the grammatical instructions. The statements of other teachers are also clear on this point.

# Chapter on Major and Sub-Periods of the Brihat Jataka
<page-num>184</page-num>
->Header: The Chapter on Major and Sub-Periods in the Brihat Jataka<-

> "Among planets occupying the same sign, only the one who is specifically the strongest becomes the harvester <note>original: 'harta' - the one who takes or distributes the portion of time</note>; the other birds <note>term: 'Vihagas' - a poetic term for planets as 'sky-travelers'</note> situated there do not."

This means—if there are many planets in one place, only the strongest among them becomes the "cooker" <note>term: 'Pachaka' - the planet that matures or 'cooks' the results of a sub-period</note> of its portion, not all of them. From this, it is proven that if there are no planets in the 1st, 5th, 9th, 4th, 8th, or 7th houses from the Lord of the Major Period <note>term: 'Dashapati'</note>, then in that planet's major period, there will be no sub-period of another planet. In that case, the Lord of the Major Period will also be the Lord of the Sub-Period. || 2 ||

**Example:** If we are to consider the sub-periods in the major period of the Sun: suppose the Ascendant, Moon, and Saturn are with the Sun. Among these, the Moon is the strongest; therefore, the Moon becomes the "cooker" of one-half (1/2) the portion. Furthermore, there are no planets in the trines <note>the 5th and 9th houses</note> or the 7th from the Sun, but Jupiter is in the 8th <note>Note: The text mentions 8th here, though standard rules often cite the 4th/8th as the 'Chaturasra' or square positions</note>; thus, it becomes the cooker of one-fourth (1/4) the portion. In this way, in the Sun's major period, the Sun (1/1), Moon (1/2), and Jupiter (1/4) become the sub-period cookers. || 3 ||

### Now, he describes the knowledge of calculating the sub-periods in the Indra-vajra meter:

**"Having reduced these positions to a common denominator, and removing the denominators, the remaining numerators are used as multipliers for the total years of the major period. The sum of these numerators becomes the divisor; the result is the division of the sub-periods."** || 4 ||

**Commentary:** The portions such as one-half (1/2) are referred to by the word "positions" <note>original: 'sthana'</note>. One should perform the "homogenization" <note>term: 'Savarna' - the mathematical process of finding a common denominator</note> of these fractional portions. By creating similarity through a common denominator, all those positions should then be stripped of their lower denominators. This means discarding the denominators. The remaining numbers on top (numerators) become the multipliers for each respective portion. The "divisor" is formed by the "sum of those" numbers—the addition of those numerators. To what do these multipliers and divisors apply? He says: to the "total years of the major period" <note>original: 'Dashabda-pinda'</note>. By this, it is said: by multiplying the major period years separately by each multiplier and dividing by the divisor, the sub-periods in years, etc., are obtained.

For example: If no other planet is situated with the Lord of the Major Period and none are in the other specified positions, then he alone is the harvester. In that case, one should place the number one (1) below the whole number (1) of the Lord. Likewise, for a half-share, one would place two (2) below the number...

---

<margin>
(1) The logic here: According to the verse "One in the same sign takes half and gives his own," etc., a planet in the same sign as the Major Lord becomes the cooker of half the sub-period time granted by the Major Lord. Similarly, a planet in a trine (5th/9th) from the Major Lord becomes the cooker of one-third (1/3) of the time. A planet in a square (4th/8th) becomes the cooker of one-fourth (1/4). One in the 7th becomes the cooker of one-seventh (1/7). First, the portion of the Major Lord is calculated, and then the portions for planets in the same sign, etc., are determined. Since the divisions of halves, etc., for those in the same sign depend on the portion that comes to the Major Lord, one must sum all portions and use a ratio to find the individual sub-period values. That is: if the sum of all portions equals the total years of the Major Lord, then what will each individual portion yield? Thus, the sub-period values are calculated.
</margin>

The arrangement is $\frac{1}{1} \mid \frac{2}{1}$. These should be multiplied by each other's denominators <note>This is the process of finding a common denominator</note>. Having done so: $\frac{1}{1} \mid \frac{2}{1}$. These are now of equal denominators; removing the denominators, we get 2 and 1. These are the multipliers. Their sum is 3; this is the divisor. Here, the life-span <note>The total period length</note> granted by the period lord is 3 years, 0 months, 0 days, 0 minutes. Multiplying this by two and dividing by three, the result obtained is 2. This is the sub-period of the primary period lord. Then again, the years etc. of the primary period lord—3 years, 0 months, 0 days, 0 minutes—multiplied by one and divided by three, the result obtained is 1 year, 0 months, 0 days, 0 minutes. This is the sub-period of the planet situated in the same sign as the period lord. Thus, the sub-period time granted by the primary period lord is reduced by half by a planet in the same sign. The sum of these two sub-period times is 3 years, 0 months, 0 days, 0 minutes, which is the original period.

Now, if some planet is situated in one of the ninth or fifth houses from the period lord, but not in the second, nor with the period lord, nor in the square houses <note>4th and 8th</note>, nor in the seventh, then the arrangement is: $\frac{1}{1} \mid \frac{1}{3}$. These, multiplied by each other's denominators, become $\frac{3}{3} \mid \frac{1}{3}$. Removing the denominators, 3 and 1 are the multipliers. 4 is the divisor. The life-span of the primary period lord is 4 years, 0 months, 0 days, 0 minutes. Multiplying this by three and dividing by four, the result is 3 years, 0 months, 0 days, 0 minutes. This is the sub-period time of the primary period lord. Then, taking this period of 4 years, 0 months, 0 days, 0 minutes, multiplying by one and dividing by four, the result is 1 year, 0 months, 0 days, 0 minutes. This is the sub-period of the planet in the trine <note>5th or 9th house</note>. Thus, the sub-period time granted by the primary period lord is reduced by one-third by a planet in a trine. The sum of these two sub-period times is 4 years, 0 months, 0 days, 0 minutes, which is the original period.

Now, if some planet is in one of the fourth or eighth houses from the period lord, but not in the second, nor with the period lord, nor in the trines, nor in the seventh, then the arrangement is: $\frac{1}{1} \mid \frac{1}{4}$.

Here, according to the rules of <term>Arithmetic</term> <note>original: "Patiganita"</note> which state "Addition and subtraction are performed on parts with equal denominators," addition or subtraction occurs only after reducing all fractional parts to a common denominator. When the common denominator is established, a denominator equal to all parts appears below them; likewise, when their sum is calculated, that same denominator appears below the sum of all parts. As shown:

| | Part | Part$^1$ | Part$^2$ | | Sum of all parts | |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| Individual fractions with common denominators | — | — | — | Sum of these = | — | By this |
| | Denom | Denom | Denom | | Denom | |

If the value of the <term>Main Period</term> <note>original: "Mula-dasha"</note> is obtained by this sum, then what is obtained by "$\frac{Part}{Denom}$"? That represents the nature of the period value:

| Main Period $\times$ Part | | Main Period $\times$ Part | |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| ——————— | = | ——————— | Because the equal denominators |
| Sum of parts / Denom | | Sum of parts | below the multiplier and divisor cancel out. |

In this way, the period value related to other fractional reducers should also be calculated. Since in calculating the period value by the <term>Rule of Three</term> <note>original: "Trairashika"</note> the denominators below the multiplier and divisor are inevitably cancelled, the denominators were discarded after the initial reduction to a common denominator; thus, everything is proven.

In this context, if the sum of the values in the same column <term>Sajatiya; of the same type, e.g., days or months</term> exceeds the standard measure (e.g., 30 days for a month), then that sum should be divided by the standard measure, and the quotient should be added to the sum of the preceding column. This should be understood for all column additions. <page-num>162</page-num>
<header>Chapter on Periods and Sub-periods in the Brihat Jataka</header>

In the process of digestion <note>original: "pachane"; here referring to the "cooking" or ripening of planetary results</note>, the sub-period results should not be declared for a planet that has not attained the status of a sub-period ruler. Only after that, the results should be declared for the one who has attained it. On this matter, others suggest giving the first sub-period to the main period lord, then to the planet in the same sign, then to those in the trine <note>1st, 5th, and 9th houses</note>, and then to the one in the seventh house. When planets are in the trine and the square <note>1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</note>, the one who is stronger among them comes first; however, this is incorrect. For the Lord Garga says: "In the beginning, the ripening of the sub-period belongs to the period lord himself. Thereafter, it should be declared according to the sequence of the period's ripening." <note>original Latin/Sanskrit quote: "Adavantardashapako bhavatyeva dashapateh..."</note> || 4 ||

**Vernacular Explanation—** According to the previous verse, for as many sub-period rulers as have obtained a position (half-share), one should equalize the denominators <note>term: Samachheda (finding a common denominator for fractions)</note> of all those parts using the method "multiplication of the other's denominator by the numerator" etc. Then, discard the denominators below and consider the numerators above as the multipliers <note>term: Gunaka</note> for the years of the period. Consider the sum of all numerators as the divisor <note>term: Bhajaka</note> to calculate the sub-period. That is, multiply the years of the period by the individual numerators and divide by the divisor (sum of numerators); the quotient will be the sub-period in years, months, etc. || 4 ||

**Example—** For instance, in the period of the Sun, the sub-period rulers' shares were equalized by multiplying the numerators by the mutual denominators. Now, by discarding the denominators below, consider the numerators 4, 2, and 1 as multipliers and their sum, 7, as the divisor. Multiplying the Sun's period years (6y 1m 22d 1h 2m 0s) by the Sun's multiplier (4) gives 24y 6m 28d 4h 8m 0s.

| | Sun | Moon | Jupiter |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Numerator | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Denominator | 1 | 2 | 4 |

| | Sun | Moon | Jupiter |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Numerator | 4 | 2 | 1 |
| Denominator | 4 | 4 | 4 |

Dividing this by the divisor (7), the resulting sub-period of the Sun in years etc. is 3y 6m 4d 6h 5m 1s. Then, multiplying the Sun's period years by 2 and dividing by 7, the result is 1y 6m 2d 1h 3m 26s; this is the Moon's sub-period within the Sun's period. Similarly, multiplying the period years by Jupiter's multiplier (1) and dividing by 7, the result is 0y 10m 16d 1h 4m 3s; this is Jupiter's sub-period. In this way, the sub-periods and the sequence of sub-period rulers in the Moon's period should be understood by equalizing denominators as before. In the period of the Ascendant <note>Lagna</note>, the sub-period sequence is Ascendant, Sun, Jupiter. In the period of Venus, by equalizing the denominators, the multipliers are 12, 6, 4, and 3, and their sum 25 is the divisor; the sub-periods are known by multiplying and dividing the years of Venus's period by these. The sub-periods of other planets should be understood in the same way. Look at the chart <note>Kundali</note> for this example. There is no planet with Mars or in its trine, square, or seventh house; therefore, in the entire period of Mars, Mars alone will be the sub-period lord. According to the verse, one should also understand the sub-sub-periods <note>term: Pratyantardasha (finer divisions of time)</note> within the sub-periods. || 4 ||

Thus, having understood the division of periods and sub-periods, it is not yet known whose period or sub-period will yield auspicious results and whose will yield inauspicious results. For that purpose, the author describes the names of the periods according to their respective results in the <term>Vaitaliya</term> <note>a specific Sanskrit poetic meter</note> verse:

> **The period of a planet that is fully powerful or in its sign of highest exaltation is called "Complete" (Sampurna). The period of a planet devoid of strength is "Empty" (Rikta). The period of a planet in its sign of fall or in a hostile sign should be known as "Inauspicious" (Anishtaphala) in the birth chart.** ||5||

Regarding "fully powerful" (<italic>Samyagbalina</italic>): In the birth chart of a person, the planet which is fully strong—meaning it possesses all the previously mentioned strengths—its period is named "Complete" (<italic>Sampurna</italic>). Not only that, but the period of a planet situated in its highest point of exaltation is also named "Complete." By saying "fully powerful" and then "in its sign of highest exaltation," the author implies that even if a planet in its highest exaltation does not possess other sources of strength, its period is still "Complete." During a "Complete" period or sub-period, a person prospers through physical health and increase in wealth. 

Now, if a planet is not possessed of all strengths but is slightly less powerful, its period is still called "Complete." If it is not at the highest point of exaltation but is simply within its exaltation sign, then its period is "Full" (<italic>Purna</italic>). In a "Full" period, one obtains wealth and health. The period of a planet devoid of strength is named "Empty" (<italic>Rikta</italic>). For one situated in its sign of fall, the period is also "Empty"...
