<page-num>164</page-num>
# Chapter on Planetary Periods and Sub-periods of the Brihat Jataka

During the period <term>Dasha</term><note>The major planetary period in a person's life</note> and sub-period <term>Antardasha</term>, one may experience loss of wealth. Regarding a planet in its "debilitated division" (<term>Nichamsha</term>): when a planet is situated in the <term>Navamsha</term><note>A one-ninth division of a zodiac sign used for precision</note> of its sign of debilitation or in the division of an enemy, its period is known to yield unfavorable results. During such an unfavorable period or sub-period, one suffers loss of wealth and ill health. On this subject, the Lord <term>Garga</term><note>An ancient sage and authority on Vedic astrology</note> says:

> "The period of a planet endowed with all strengths and situated in its highest exaltation is known as **Sampurna** (Complete); it increases wealth and health. The period of a planet devoid of all strengths and situated in its sign of debilitation is known as **Rikta** (Empty); it destroys wealth and health. The period of a planet in its sign of exaltation but possessing only some strength is known as **Purna** (Full); it is auspicious and increases wealth. The period of a planet in its deepest debilitation or in an enemy's division is called **Anishta** (Unfavorable); it increases disease and misfortune." ||5||

**Language—** At the time of birth, a planet that is endowed with all strengths (positional, etc.) and is in its highest exaltation has a period called **Sampurna**. This brings auspicious results in every way. Conversely, a planet devoid of all strengths, in its deepest debilitation, or in an enemy's division has a period called **Rikta**, which gives inauspicious results in every way. ||5||

**Special Meaning—** Planets primarily possess four types of strength (<term>Balas</term>): Positional (<term>Sthana</term>), Motional (<term>Chesta</term>), Temporal (<term>Kala</term>), and Directional (<term>Disha</term>). When endowed with all four, a planet is called "completely strong." Lacking all four, it is called "weak." It follows that if a planet has four strengths and is exalted, it gives 100% good results; with three strengths, 75%; with two strengths, 50%; and with one strength, 25% good results. See the quote by Garga in the Sanskrit commentary.

->Now, the names of the periods and sub-periods are stated again in the <term>Indra-vajra</term> meter:<-

<margin><unclear>me</unclear></margin>
> **The period of a planet falling from its exaltation is called Avarohini (Descending). It is Madhya (Middling) if the planet is in a friend's or its own exaltation division. The period of a planet rising from its debilitation is Arohi (Ascending), but it is Adhama (Low/Vile) if the planet is in its debilitation or an enemy's sign or division. |6|**

"Falling" (<italic>Bhrashtasya</italic>) means a planet that has moved away from its point of highest exaltation is designated as **Avarohini**. This period is known by the name "Descending." From the point of highest exaltation until the point of deepest debilitation—the six signs in between—the period or sub-period given by a planet situated there is called Avarohini. This is because it is conceptualized as "falling" or descending daily from its peak. Until it reaches deepest debilitation, the Avarohini period yields "low" results. As will be said later: "The results are in accordance with the names." Regarding "It is **Madhya** (Middling) if in a friend's or exaltation division": if that same descending planet is situated in a friend's division (<term>Mitramsha</term>), the period it gives is called Madhya...

It cites the sage Garga to explain how the four types of planetary strength (Balas) mathematically determine the auspiciousness of a life period.</summary>

<page-num>165</page-num>
<header>Page 165 — Including the Sanskrit Commentary of Bhattotpala with Hindi Translation</header>

It occurs. In this manner, in whichever sign a planet is situated in its own <term>Navamsha</term><note>A one-ninth subdivision of a zodiac sign, crucial for determining a planet's true strength</note>, the <term>Dasha</term><note>Planetary period or life-stage ruled by a specific planet</note> is considered "middling." Similarly, in whichever sign it is situated in its own exaltation Navamsha, the Dasha is also middling. The period known as *Arohini* (Ascending) occurs as follows: starting from the degree of deep debilitation up to the degree of deep exaltation—within these six signs—the Dasha or sub-period given by a planet situated there is called *Arohini*. This is because from the point of deep debilitation, the planet is conceptualized as "ascending" day by day until it reaches deep exaltation. The *Arohini* Dasha yields excellent results. Regarding the phrase "in the Navamsha of a debilitated or enemy sign": that same *Arohini* planet, if situated in the Navamsha of its debilitated sign, gives a Dasha called *Adhama* (Low/Degraded). Likewise, in whichever sign it is, if situated in an enemy's Navamsha, the Dasha is also *Adhama*. Previously it was said that a Dasha given by a planet in an enemy's Navamsha is "fruitless"; now it is called "low." What is the distinction? It is explained here: an *Avarohini* (Descending) Dasha, even when given by a planet in an enemy's Navamsha, should be known as having "undesirable results." The *Arohini* is "low." What is the difference in their fruits? It is said: "Undesirable results" provide inauspicious fruits. "Low" provides the same inauspiciousness, but to a lesser degree. In this way, when the *Arohini* designation becomes the *Adhama* designation, it then acquires the name of "undesirable fruit." When the *Arohini* is designated as "middling," it should be known by the name "Full." On this matter, the Lord Garga states:

->“The Dasha of a planet situated between exaltation and debilitation is *Avarohini* (Descending).<-
->In that period, a person obtains little fruit, and auspiciousness comes only through distress.<-
->The Dasha of a planet in a friend's, exaltation, or own Navamsha is middling and yields middling fruits.<-
->The Dasha of a planet moving from debilitation toward exaltation is called *Arohini* (Ascending) and is excellent.<-
->That same Dasha is called *Adhama* (Low) if the planet is in a debilitated sign or Navamsha.<-
->If the *Avarohini* Dasha is also *Adhama*, it then yields painful results.<-
->The *Arohini* Dasha with middling fruits is proclaimed as 'Complete' (*Sampurna*).”<- || 6 ||

**Vernacular Translation—** The Dasha of a planet that has passed its point of deep exaltation and is moving toward debilitation is called *Avarohini*. Because its motion is directed toward debilitation, it is inauspicious. However, if the planet is in a friendly sign's Navamsha or its own exaltation Navamsha, even the *Avarohini* Dasha gives middling results. Furthermore, the Dasha of a planet that has passed its point of deep debilitation and is moving toward exaltation is called *Arohini*; because its motion is directed toward exaltation, it is auspicious. But if the planet is in its debilitated Navamsha or an enemy's Navamsha, even the *Arohini* Dasha gives inauspicious results. From this, it is proven that if a planet is in its own Navamsha or its exaltation Navamsha, the *Arohini* Dasha is especially auspicious. || 6 ||

### Now, he describes the designations of periods and sub-periods again in the Upajati meter—

> **If a planet is situated in a favorable house but occupies a debilitated or inimical sign in the divisional chart (Navamsha), the results are declared to be mixed. I shall now describe the results according to their designations in these periods as they apply. ||7||**

**Commentary:** "Debilitated etc." If a period or sub-period is given by a planet situated in favorable houses—such as its sign of exaltation, its root-trine <note>Moolatrikona: a specific favorable area of a sign</note>, its own sign, or a friend's sign—but that planet simultaneously occupies a debilitated sign or an enemy's sign in the Navamsha <note>the 1/9th divisional chart used to assess a planet's true strength</note>, the result is only mixed. Mixed results provide both auspicious and inauspicious effects. For example, one might predict the acquisition of wealth accompanied by disease. Furthermore, if a planet is in an unfavorable sign (an enemy's or debilitated sign) but occupies its exaltation, friend's sign, root-trine, or its own Vargottama Navamsha <note>where the planet is in the same sign in both the main and divisional charts</note>, the result is also mixed. The results should be understood as corresponding to their names during their sub-periods. For instance: "Complete" gives extremely excellent results; "Full" gives excellent results; "Mean" gives small auspicious results; "Empty" or "Depriving" gives undesirable results; and "Mixed" gives both good and bad results.

Now, regarding the status of these periods. The word "Now" implies sequence. I shall describe the use of these planets, starting with the Sun, in their respective periods hereafter. I will explain them in the manner they are applied—specifically, which result is applicable in whose sub-period. ||7||

**Vernacular Translation**— If a planet is in a favorable (exalted, etc.) sign but in a debilitated or enemy sign in the Navamsha, its result is mixed (both good and bad). Moving forward, the results of these (the planets including the Ascendant) in their own periods are similar to their designations; these are described as appropriate. ||7||

**Special Meaning**— The core idea is that one must declare results after understanding the status of planets from both their zodiac sign and their Navamsha positions. As stated by Lord Garga—see the Sanskrit commentary on the sixth verse. ||7||

If the Ascendant falls in a dual (mutable) sign, the periods are known as bad, middling, and honored according to the sequence of the decans <note>Drekkana: a 10-degree division of a sign</note>. For one born in the first decan, it is bad (inauspicious); in the second decan, it is middling (mixed); in the third decan, it is honored (excellent). In a movable sign, it is the reverse: for one born in the first decan, it is honored; in the second, middling; and in the third, bad/undesirable. "Inauspicious, desired, and equal in fixed signs in order": in a fixed sign, the first decan...

...maintains stability for as long as the periods and sub-periods related to that planet last. During that time, the "ripening" <note>Sanskrit: *paktih*; refers to the fruition of karmic results</note> of the period yields full results. This means that as long as the sequence continues in order, the results remain auspicious. On this point, some authorities argue: if the period is auspicious according to previous rules, it grants exceedingly good results; otherwise, if inauspicious, it grants exceedingly bad results. However, this view is incorrect. As **Yavanesvara** <note>The "Lord of the Greeks," an influential early authority in Indian astrology</note> states:

> "A planet's period is best during its own natural age."

**Satya** <note>Satyacharya, a highly respected traditional astrologer</note> says the same: "The Moon's natural age is one year; Mars is three years; Mercury is twelve years; Venus is thirty-two; and Jupiter is said to be half of a hundred (50). The Sun is seventy years, and Saturn is one hundred and twenty years. These intervals of age are the natural time (*naisargika kala*) of their respective periods. Upon reaching their own specific age, the planets provide protection, nourishment, activity, and temperament to living beings respectively."

Now, regarding the natural period of the **Ascendant** <term>Lagna: the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at birth</term> according to the opinion of the **Ancient Greeks** <note>original: *Purana-Yavana*</note>: the Ascendant's period comes at the end. If someone’s lifespan exceeds one hundred and twenty years, that entire remaining time belongs naturally to the Ascendant. In that time, according to the opinion of the Ancient Greeks, the Ascendant's period is auspicious. 

How do we know it is after one hundred and twenty years? It is explained that before that time, the years are occupied by the other planets, leaving no room for the Ascendant. 

But another might ask: "Does this mean that for someone whose life does not exceed one hundred and twenty years, there is no natural period for the Ascendant?" The answer is: indeed, there is not. Just as for someone who does not live past seventy, there is no natural period for Saturn; and for someone who does not live past fifty, there is nothing for the Sun. This logic should be applied to the others as well. 

One might then ask: "If one hundred and twenty years is the maximum lifespan, and there is no life beyond that, what is the point of the Ascendant's natural period?" This was explained previously: the one hundred and twenty years is a maximum lifespan used for the "Rule of Three" <note>A mathematical proportion used to calculate longevity</note> and for determining the lifespan of animals like horses. Life can indeed exist beyond that measure. 

For example: if someone is born when **Pisces** is the Ascendant and is strong, specifically at the end of a Pisces subdivision (*Anshaka*), and all other planets are also situated in Pisces subdivisions—some in exaltation and some in retrograde—then the Pisces Ascendant grants twelve years. Because it is strong, it grants another twelve. Each planet, being at the end of a Pisces subdivision, grants twelve years. Because they are retrograde or exalted, those years are tripled to thirty-six (except for the Sun). The Sun, situated in the middle degrees of Aries, grants twenty-seven years. Thus, for the six planets starting with the Moon, the total becomes two hundred and sixteen...

...can go into the <term>Navamsha</term><note>A one-ninth divisional chart used for precision in Vedic astrology</note> of Pisces. Therefore, if the Sun is in the final Navamsha of Aries, and all planets are in the first half of the zodiac, and the <term>Lagna</term><note>The Ascendant or rising sign</note> is aspected by or conjoined with its own lord and Jupiter or Mercury, then in this situation—according to the opinion of <term>Satyacharya</term><note>An ancient authority on astrology often cited by Varahamihira</note>—the longevity contributed by the Sun is tripled to 27 years. -> Now, he describes the knowledge of good and bad results of the periods and sub-periods in the <term>Shardulavikridita</term><note>A specific Sanskrit poetic meter</note> meter: <-

> **When the lord of the period is in the Ascendant, or in a friend's sign, or in its own divisional varga, or in a benefic sign, the period started provides auspicious results. This is also true if the period lord is in the 3rd, 10th, 6th, or 11th houses from the Ascendant. If the Moon is situated in a friendly sign, exaltation sign, an Upachaya house (3, 6, 10, 11), a trine (1, 5, 9), or the 7th house relative to the lord of the period, it brings about the realization of good results; otherwise, the results are evil.** || 10 ||

Regarding "the lord of the period" (<term>Pakasvami</term>): There are four measurements of time: Solar, Savana (terrestrial), Lunar, and Sidereal. Among these, the **Solar** measurement is the movement of the Sun through the zodiac. The time it takes for the Sun to move one degree is a Solar day. The time it takes to move through the twelve signs is a Solar year. That consists of 365 days and 15.5 <term>ghatikas</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. 

**Savana** is from sunrise to sunrise. From one sunrise to the next sunrise is a Savana day-and-night (<term>Ahoratra</term>). That is a day-and-night of 60 ghatikas. Thirty such days make a month. Twelve such months make a year. Thus, a Savana year consists of 360 days. 

**Lunar** is the movement of the <term>Tithi</term><note>A lunar day based on the angle between the Sun and Moon</note>. By its own measure, it is 360 units, but when measured by Savana days, a lunar year is 354 days. Thus, Solar, Savana, and Lunar measurements each consist of 360 units by their own respective scales. 

**Sidereal** (<term>Nakshatra</term>) is the Moon's movement through the constellations. A month consists of 27 days. A year is said to be 324 days. 

<insert>As stated: "The movement of the Sun through one degree is a Solar day-and-night; a Lunar day is a Tithi. The movement of the Moon through a constellation is known as Sidereal. Savana is the duration from sunrise to sunrise for planets and stars. In Sidereal measure, a month is 27 days. In the remaining measures, a month is specified as 30 days."</insert> 

Therefore, the calculation of longevity must be done using the **Savana** measure. This is because the longevity must be calculated after performing necessary subtractions and additions, and that is based on the Savana measure. By Solar measure, the transition (<term>Sankranti</term>)...

# Page 201
### With the Sanskrit Commentary of Bhattotpala and Hindi Translation

...the month ends at that limit. A **Savana** <note>civil or terrestrial</note> month consists of thirty nights. A **Lunar** month ends with the New Moon. A **Sidereal** month ends with the constellation Revati. The **Solar** measure, when combined with intercalary months <note>Adhimasa</note>, becomes the Lunar measure. The Lunar measure, when reduced by omitted lunar days <note>Avama-ratra</note>, becomes the Savana measure. By the term "Lunar," the Sidereal is also implied. As it has been said:

> "The sum of Yugas, years, and months in Solar measure, plus the intercalary months, is the Lunar measure. Subtracting the omitted days gives the Savana measure; the Lunar year is the year combined with these cycles."

Thus, the procedure for determining life expectancy <note>Ayurdaya</note> is performed using the Savana measure, purified by additions and subtractions. 

So also says the venerable **Garga** in the *Mayurachitrakam*:
> "The division of life expectancy, the performance of penance <note>Prayashchitta</note>, and the observance of sacrificial sessions <note>Sattras</note> must be done by the Savana measure alone."

(1) Now, an objection: In the *Pulisha-Tantra*, a day-and-night measured from one sunrise to the next is read as a **Solar** day-and-night:
> "The numbers 1, 7, 8, 9, 7, 6, 2 multiplied by a hundred are by Solar measure..."

This is known only to Pulisha. Because, excluding the *Pulisha-Tantra*, in all **Siddhantas** <note>astronomical treatises</note> and Tantras, the Solar measure plus intercalary months is Lunar, and the Lunar minus omitted days is Savana. Thus, in all **Samhitas** <note>compendiums</note>, the Savana measure is purified by additions and subtractions, and the name for a day-and-night from sunrise to sunrise is the **Savana Day-and-Night**. 

So says the venerable **Parashara**: "The Savana day-and-night." And **Garga**: "A month is known as Savana by thirty sunrises." Likewise, the illustrious **Brahmagupta**: "Savana is from sunrise to sunrise." 

Thus, at the time of a person's birth, having calculated the **Ahargana** <note>term: Ahargana; the total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch to the current date</note> in Savana measure, and from that determining the specific Tithi <note>lunar day</note>, Nakshatra <note>constellation</note>, and the positions of the planets and the Ascendant <note>Lagna</note> for that moment, one should then calculate the major and minor planetary periods <note>Dasha and Antardasha</note>. Then, the results of the upcoming periods should be predicted. 

In that process, first calculate the *Ahargana* for the birth moment. Then, convert the duration of the minor periods (years, etc.) into days and add them: multiply the years by twelve, add the months, multiply again by thirty, and add the remaining days. In this way, the period is expressed in days. By adding these days (including fractions) to the birth *Ahargana*, the new *Ahargana* is found. If the initial time starts at a certain Ghatika <note>unit of 24 minutes</note>, the calculation should be made from the preceding midnight. From this, one should bring forth the desired day-measure using the teacher's formula:

> "The day-count <note>Dyugana</note> placed below, multiplied by the lunar days... [technical calculation involving 7, 6, 9, 2] ...minus the intercalary days is the Lunar measure."

This is derived from the *Khandakhadyaka* treatise. Regarding what constitutes the Solar day-count, he says:
> "The Shaka era minus 587, multiplied by twelve, combined with the months starting from Chaitra, multiplied by thirty, and added to the Tithis..."

(1) The illustrious **Bhaskaracharya** also states in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*:
> "Penance, impurity periods <note>Sutaka</note>, medical treatment, and the start/end of days—these are from Savana measure."

**Shripati** also says: 
> "Penance, impurity, medicine, sacrifice, and the sequence of weekdays; but in this science, the movement of the planets must be known from the Savana measure of the Sun."

# Chapter on Periods and Sub-periods in the Brihat Jataka

Thus, by dividing this by three hundred and sixty, the quotient gives the "Karana years" <note>astronomical years used in calculation</note>. The remainder, divided by thirty, gives the months starting from the bright half of Chaitra. The remaining figures are the lunar days (tithis) starting from the bright half of the current month. By adding 587 <note>original: "agavasusharan" - a numerical code where aga=7, vasu=8, shara=5, read right-to-left as 587</note> to these Karana years, the elapsed Shaka era is found. On that Shaka year, in that month, and on that day, the "heap of days" <term>Ahargana: the total number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch</term> is established.

At that point, the entry into the major period (Dasha) occurs. To find the entry into a sub-period (Antardasha), one should convert that time into days and add it. In this manner, all sub-periods should be added according to their respective shares. Then, one should calculate the positions of the planets and the Ascendant (Lagna).

Alternatively, there is another method for calculating time. When calculating for the Sun, the number of completed revolutions represents the years elapsed since the start of the calculation. By adding the Shaka era used in the calculation to these, the desired Shaka year is found. In the current year, the number of zodiac signs traversed by the true Sun indicates the number of solar months passed. Whether it is the bright or dark fortnight, and the specific lunar day and mansion, is known from the positions of the Moon and Sun. Regarding the "Lord of the Ripening" <note>the planet whose period is currently active</note> and so on:

The planet whose sub-period is beginning is called the **Lord of the Ripening** (*Pakasvami*). He remains the Lord of the Ripening for the duration of his sub-period. If that Lord of the Ripening is situated in the Ascendant (Lagna) at the moment the sub-period begins, then the sub-period associated with him will be auspicious and yield good results. Alternatively, if the "Varga" <note>divisional strength</note> of the major period lord—as explained previously—is rising in the Ascendant, it is auspicious. Or, if a planet that is a "temporary friend" of the Lord of the Ripening is in the Ascendant at the time of entry, the period should be declared auspicious. Furthermore, if any other benefic planet (a "gentle" planet) is in the Ascendant at that time, the start is indeed auspicious. Or, if the Lord of the Period (*Pakapa*) is situated in the 3rd, 10th, 6th, or 11th houses <note>original: "tridashashadlabha"</note> from the temporary Ascendant, the period should be declared auspicious.

Although it is stated generally here that the period will be auspicious, one must also consider this:

> "In the sub-period of an enemy or a great enemy, the results obtained are undesirable. Even a great friend, when entering the sub-period of a friend, becomes auspicious. A neutral planet entering a neutral sub-period gives results as previously described."

This must also be reflected upon. One might wonder: in an auspicious sub-period, are good results obtained continuously at all times? Or in an inauspicious sub-period, are bad results obtained only on certain days? To clear this doubt regarding both cases, the text says "from a friend's house" and so on. When the Moon, in its transit through the various signs, enters a sign whose lord is a temporary friend of the **Lord of the Ripening** (*Pakesvara*), it makes the good results manifest. Here, on whichever day the Moon is in a particular house due to its transit, if the lord of that house is a temporary friend of the Period Lord on that day, then the Moon is said to be in the "friend's territory" of the Period Lord.

It should be understood. Likewise, the Moon, when situated in its own sign of exaltation <note>the sign where a planet is at its maximum strength</note> or its own sign, provides indications of good results for the Lord of the Period <term>Pakapati: the planet currently ruling a specific span of time in a person's life</term>. Not only that, but as long as the Moon is in an Upachaya house <note>houses of improvement: the 3rd, 6th, 10th, and 11th</note> relative to the Lord of the Period—specifically in any of the third, sixth, eleventh, or tenth positions—or in a Trine <note>Trikona: the 1st, 5th, or 9th houses</note>, or in the seventh house <note>Madana: the house of partnerships</note>; when the Moon is in any of these specified positions, it indicates good results during a favorable period. If it is asked how these results are known, it is said: the Moon, situated in a friend's sign, exaltation, an Upachaya house, a Trine, or the seventh house, indicates the good results arising from whatever "House" <term>Bhava: one of the twelve areas of life, such as wealth or health</term> that sign represented at the time of birth. This is especially true as described for the period. Therefore, contrary to what has been said, if the Moon is in the house of an enemy of the Lord of the Period, or in its sign of debilitation <note>Neecha: the sign where a planet is weakest</note>, or in the same sign as the Lord of the Period, or in any of the second, fourth, eighth, or twelfth houses, then even in a favorable period, it manifests sinful <note>unfavorable</note> results. Even the undesirable results arising from the Ashtakavarga <note>a system of points based on planetary positions</note> are turned to good indications in a mixed period if the Moon is in a friend's sign, exaltation, or Upachaya; if in an enemy's sign or debilitation, it indicates unfavorable results. And so says the Lord Garga:

> "The sign in which the Moon <note>original: 'Shitanshu', the cool-rayed one</note> is situated is declared to be a doer of good. Whatever 'House' that sign was at the time of birth, the result pertains to that. Happiness related to the body and other matters should be predicted according to its strength. If it is in an unfavorable sign, the results for those Houses are not auspicious."

10.

**Vernacular Commentary—** If the Lord of the Period <term>Pakasvami</term> is in the Ascendant <note>Lagna: the sign rising on the eastern horizon</note>, or if the friends of the Lord of the Period are in the Ascendant, or if the divisions <note>Varga: sub-divisional charts like Hora</note> of the Lord of the Period or its friends, or the divisions of a benefic planet or a friend are in the Ascendant, or if the Lord of the Period is in the division of a benefic friend and is in the 3rd, 6th, 10th, or 11th house from the Ascendant, then a period starting at such a time will give auspicious results. Otherwise, due to the influence of position and other factors, the period gives middling or inauspicious results. Due to its constant movement, whenever the Moon enters a sign friendly to the Lord of the Period, its sign of exaltation, or an Upachaya (3, 6, 10, 11) position from the Lord of the Period, it gives auspicious results. Otherwise (meaning when the Moon goes to an enemy's sign, a sign of debilitation, or a house other than an Upachaya), it produces inauspicious results. || 10 ||

**Special Meaning—** At the time a period begins, one should calculate the exact positions of the planets and the Ascendant to understand the auspicious or inauspicious results of the period. For the logical method of knowing the start time of a period and a clear example, see my commentary (*Sarvamanorama*) on the *Keshaviya Jataka Paddhati*. The years of the period are taken according to the Savana measurement <note>a solar-day based calendar system</note>. As per the statement of Lord Garga—

> "The division of the life span <term>Ayurdaya: the calculation of longevity</term> and the performance of expiatory rites <term>Prayashchitta: rituals performed to neutralize bad karma</term>, as well as the observance of sacrificial sessions, must be calculated using the Savana measurement of time <note>Savana refers to a 360-day year where each day is exactly 24 hours from sunrise to sunrise</note>." The meaning is clear.

The period of the first "Lord of the Dasha" <term>Dashapati: the planet ruling a specific period of life</term> begins exactly at the moment of birth. Therefore, the planetary positions and the Ascendant <term>Lagna: the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</term> at birth are also the starting conditions for the first Dasha. After that, one must determine the starting times for the sub-periods of other planets to judge their effects as previously described. 

For example, in the illustration shown, the first period is that of the Sun. The Ascendant at birth is the same as the Ascendant at the start of the Dasha. Now, how will the Sun's period be? To judge this, look at the birth chart. Here, the Sun (the Lord of the Dasha) is placed in a friendly sign; therefore, according to the rule "when the lord of the ripening period is in the Ascendant" <note>original Sanskrit: "Pakasvamini lagnage"</note>, the Sun's period is proven to yield extremely auspicious results for the native. This means that from the time of birth until the end of the Sun's period (6 years, 1 month, 22 days, 12 minutes), the native will attain all kinds of happiness. Furthermore, the Moon is in the exaltation sign of the Dasha Lord at the time of birth, making this time highly favorable. 

In the same way, moving forward, whenever the Moon enters a sign friendly to the Sun, an exaltation sign, or an Upachaya house <note>The 3rd, 6th, 10th, and 11th houses, associated with growth and improvement</note>, one should understand that there will be a specific gain of happiness. The specific auspicious results will relate to whichever house that sign occupied in the original birth chart. Conversely, when the Moon falls in an inauspicious position relative to the Sun, the native will experience unfavorable results related to the house that the Moon's current sign occupied at birth.

->**Knowledge of auspiciousness based on the sign occupied by the Moon at the start of a sub-period**<-
->**The author states this in the Shardulavikridita meter:**<-

**If a sub-period begins while the Moon is in its own sign (Cancer), it brings honor, wealth, and happiness. In the signs of Mars (Aries/Scorpio), it ruins women. In the signs of Mercury (Gemini/Virgo), it grants knowledge, friends, and wealth. In the sign of the Sun (Leo), it leads to labor in forests, forts, and roads. In the signs of Venus (Taurus/Libra), it provides food. In the signs of Saturn (Capricorn/Aquarius), it brings a low-status wife. In the signs of Jupiter (Sagittarius/Pisces), it brings honor, wealth, and happiness.**

"If the Moon starts..." <note>original: "Prarabdha himagau"</note> means: at the moment any planet's sub-period <term>Antardasha</term> begins, if the Moon is in its own sign (Cancer), it brings happiness, wealth, and honor. "Happiness" refers to a state of comfort, "Wealth" to money, and "Honor" to respect or worship—

**Vernacular Explanation**—In the period or sub-period of the Sun situated in an auspicious house, wealth is gained from perfumes <note>or tiger-claws/nails used in medicine</note>, ivory, skins of deer or tigers, gold, fierce deeds, roads <note>the authority to build or manage highways</note>, the king, and war. Furthermore, there is an increase in mental firmness, patience, love for continuous industry, fame, and majesty. 

If the Sun is in an inauspicious house, various calamities arise from the wife, children, wealth, enemies, weapons, fire, and the king. Also, there is "renunciation" (excessive expenditure), a love for sinful acts, quarrels with one's own servants, and pain or disease in the heart and stomach. That is to say, when the Sun is in a neutral position, its period (the mixed period) yields mixed results (both good and bad). ||12||

As shown in the previous example: the Sun and Venus are exalted and are behind their respective degrees of deep exaltation; therefore, this is an **Ascending Period** <term>Arohini Dasha: a period where the planet's influence is increasing in strength</term>. Thus, the periods of both will give excellent results. Conversely, Mars has passed its point of exaltation and is approaching its debilitation; therefore, it is called a **Descending Period** <term>Avarohini Dasha: a period where the planet's influence is fading</term>. Since Mars is also in a neutral sign, its period will generally give inauspicious results. One should evaluate other planets in this same manner. ||12||

## Commentary by Bhattotpala with Hindi Translation

**Harshness and so forth:** "Harshness" refers to cruelty in speech. "Exertion" means fatigue. "Bondage" refers to imprisonment. "Mental grief" is the distress of the mind; these things occur. ### Now, the good and bad results during the period of Jupiter are told in the Shardulavikridita meter:

->In Jupiter’s period, there is the rise of honor and virtue, growth of intellect, beauty, and progress through valor.<-
->Wealth comes through greatness, effort, counsel, policy, kings, and the study of sacred texts.<-
->There is an abundance of gold, horses, children, elephants, and clothes, and affection with good kings.<-
->But also exhaustion from deep, subtle contemplation, ear disease, and enmity with those outside the faith.<- ||16||

**In Jupiter’s period:** This refers to the period <term>Dasha; the major planetary cycle in Vedic astrology</term> belonging to Jupiter <note>Sanskrit: *Jiva*</note>. In that period, there is the "rise of honor and virtues"—honor meaning worship or respect, and virtues meaning learning, heroism, and so on; these manifest. "Growth of intellect" is the increase of wisdom. "Beauty" is loveliness. "Progress through valor" is advancement through manly effort. "Influence" is the fear felt by enemies. "Greatness" is the disposition to help others, though some say it means pride. "Effort" is the quality of industriousness. "Through mantras" refers to Vedic or other sacred chants. "Wealth through policy, kings, study, and counsel"—Policy refers to the science of politics taught by Chanakya or others. "Kings" means wealth through serving the monarch. "Study" <note>Sanskrit: *svadhyaya*</note> means through teaching or recitation. "Counsel" or "Mantra" means through the chanting of secret prayers. Through these, one obtains wealth. "Gold," "Horses," "Children" (sons), "Elephants," and "Clothes"—there is an abundance of these. One gains "affection" or friendship with "good kings" (virtuous rulers). This occurs in a favorable period. 

Now, for the unfavorable period: "Exhaustion from subtle contemplation" and so forth. There is "exertion" or fatigue for one who "contemplates" or reasons out "subtle" and "deep" matters. This means one who investigates things that are very fine, exhausting to the mind, and hidden. "Ear disease" refers to ailments of the hearing. "Enmity with those outside the faith" <note>Sanskrit: *vidharmashritaih*</note> means conflict with men who stand outside the established religious law. In a mixed period, both results occur. Thus ends the results of the sub-period of Jupiter. ||16||

**Vernacular Translation—** In the period of a well-placed Jupiter, there is an increase in respect and virtues in the world, growth of intellect, beauty, progress through bravery, philanthropy, industry...

# Brihat Jataka: Chapter on Major and Minor Periods

<page-num>210</page-num>
->The Chapter on Major and Minor Periods<-

Through mantras <note>sacred chants or counsel</note>, policy, the king, study, and the recitation of prayers, wealth is gained. There is an increase in gold, clothing, horses, elephants, and sons, as well as affection from the king. In the period of an inauspicious Jupiter, there is exhaustion from debating subtle subjects, ear diseases, and associations with the unrighteous. ||16||

*Now, the auspicious and inauspicious effects during the period of Venus are told in the Shardulavikridita meter:*

**During the period of Venus, there is a fondness for music, joy, fragrant substances, fine food, drinks, and garments. One gains women, gems, splendor, tools of desire <note>luxuries like fine bedding</note>, knowledge, and the arrival of dear friends. There is skill in buying and selling, success in agriculture, the discovery of hidden treasure, and the arrival of wealth. However, there is enmity with groups, kings, hunters, and the lawless, and grief arises from one's own affections.** ||17||

Regarding "During the period of Venus" <note>original: "Shaukryam"</note> || This is the period belonging to Venus. In this period: fondness for music; joy; fragrant substances <note>perfumes</note>; food; drinks <note>liquors or beverages</note>; garments; women; gems; splendor; tools of desire <note>objects for sensual enjoyment such as beds</note>; knowledge of the Yoga Shastras <note>treatises on union or discipline</note>; and the arrival of dear friends are obtained. Skill <note>original: "Kaushalyam"</note> means being educated or excelling in desired actions. Buying and selling refers to trade. Agriculture refers to farming. Treasure <note>original: "Nidhi"</note> refers to wealth deposited in the earth by others; its acquisition is a gain. These occur in an auspicious period. Now, for the inauspicious period: "with groups, kings..." Enmity is gained with groups of people, with the ruler of the earth <note>the king</note>, with hunters <note>those who live by killing creatures</note>, and with those devoid of righteousness <note>those addicted to sin</note>. "Grief from affection" means sorrows arise from love. Where there is attachment, one experiences the resulting grief. In a mixed period, both effects occur. Thus ends the result of the major and minor periods of Venus. || 17 ||

**Vernacular Translation** — In the period of Venus situated in an auspicious house, there is joy from an attachment to music, fragrant substances, good food, drinks, clothing, women, gems, beauty, sensual luxuries, knowledge, and meetings with beloved friends. There is cleverness in trade, profit from farming, the discovery of treasure <note>wealth hidden in the ground</note>, and gain of wealth through other means. In the period of Venus situated in an inauspicious house, there is enmity with crowds, the king, hunters <note>outcastes or those of low birth</note>, and the unrighteous, and grief follows after forming attachments. ||17||

### Now, he describes the good and bad results during the period of Saturn in the Shardulavikridita meter—

**Upon reaching the period of Saturn, one gains donkeys, camels, birds, she-buffaloes, and elderly women; honor arising from authority over guilds, villages, and cities; and the acquisition of coarse grains. One also encounters afflictions of phlegm, envy, wind, anger, delusion, and impurity, as well as drowsiness, exhaustion, and insults from servants, children, and spouses, or even the loss of a limb. || 18 ||**

Regarding "Upon reaching the period of Saturn" (Saurim): In the period of Saturn, one obtains donkeys, camels, birds such as hawks, the well-known she-buffalo, and elderly women. A "guild" (shreni) refers to a collection of many people of the same class; one is appointed to authority over them. One receives honor arising from authority over a guild, village, or city. There is the acquisition of "coarse grains" (kudhanya) such as kodo millet. These occur in a favorable period. 

Now, for the unfavorable period: "phlegm, envy," etc. Affliction by phlegm (kapha); by envy or jealousy; by wind (the vata humor); by anger; by delusion or mental confusion; and by impurity or filthiness. "Drowsiness" (tandra) exists between sleep and laziness. Its definition is:

> "A state of agitation in the heart, heaviness of speech and senses, and a lack of clarity in the mind and intellect—this is known as the definition of drowsiness."

One experiences exhaustion or fatigue. One receives "insults" or scolding from servants (laborers), from children (sons and daughters), and from spouses (wives). "Loss of a limb" (vyangatam) refers to the cutting off of a limb or its impairment by disease. In a mixed period, both types of results occur. Thus ends the results for the period and sub-periods of Saturn. || 18 ||

**Vernacular Translation**— In the period of a favorably placed Saturn, one gains the company of donkeys, camels, birds, buffaloes, and elderly women; respect through authority over public society, villages, and cities; and the acquisition of coarse grains like kodo, madua, and bajra. In the period of an unfavorable Saturn, one encounters distress from phlegm, envy, wind, anger, delusion, and impurity; drowsiness and exhaustion; and disrespect from servants, children, and wives, as well as the breaking of limbs. || 18 ||

Now, in a single verse, he describes the division of good and bad results across all periods, as well as the results of the Ascendant period, in the Upajati meter—

->**In auspicious periods, the planets produce good results;**<-
->**In those designated as inauspicious, they produce bad results.**<-
->**In mixed periods, the results are mixed;**<-
->**The result of the Ascendant period is equal to that of its Lord. || 19 ||**<-

<note>The "Ascendant period" (Hora-phalam) refers to a specific timing technique where the results are judged based on the planet that rules the rising sign at birth.</note>

# Page 212
## Chapter on Planetary Periods and Sub-periods in the Brihat Jataka

Regarding the periods: The auspicious, inauspicious, or mixed nature of the planetary periods has been stated previously. Similarly, those planets which, at the time of birth, are situated in the <term>Upachaya</term><note>Houses of increase: the 3rd, 6th, 10th, and 11th houses</note> houses, possess clear forms, and have distinct motions—their periods are auspicious. Those planets situated in the <term>Apachaya</term><note>Houses of decrease/non-increase</note> houses, which are afflicted, parched, or of small form—their periods are inauspicious. And so says Yavaneshvara <note>The "Lord of the Greeks," an early authority in Indian astrology</note>:

> "Whichever among the Moon, the Sun, or the Ascendant possesses the greatest strength through its associations at that time, its period is considered the first; the others follow in order of their remaining strength. The planet that is advanced in age or was the first to rise is designated as the first lord of the period. If a planet is strong and situated in a <term>Kendra</term><note>Angular houses: 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th</note>, it comes first, and the others follow as prescribed. A period is best when it occurs during the planet's own natural age, or when the planet is in its sign of exaltation or possesses temporal strength. It is middling when in its <term>Moolatrikona</term><note>A specific favorable sign position</note>, its own house, or a friend's house, or the house occupied at birth. A period is said to be full of many faults if the planet is in its sign of fall, an enemy's sign, or a house that is destroyed, discolored, or parched, or if it is the lord of the 8th or 6th house from the lord of the birth."

Thus, in favorable and beautiful periods, the planets produce only auspicious results. The auspicious or inauspicious results that have been declared for the commencement of a period are exactly what occur. No others. In periods designated as undesirable, only inauspicious and undesirable things happen. In mixed periods, the results are indeed mixed. This has been explained by us in every verse. And so says Satya:

> "Planets situated in the houses of increase at birth, moving clockwise and possessing beautiful forms, bestow the best results when they reach their respective periods. Those afflicted by others, parched, of small form, and situated in houses of decrease, do not grant the desired results of their periods to people. The result of the <term>Hora</term><note>The hour or the Ascendant</note> should be declared equal to that of the Lord of the Ascendant. For example, the results of the period of Mars for one born with Aries as the Ascendant, or the results of the period of Venus for one born with Taurus as the Ascendant. The same should be said for others; however, due to the influence of the <term>Drekkana</term><note>A 10-degree subdivision of a sign</note>, the result is auspicious if the Ascendant period is auspicious, and inauspicious if it is inauspicious. In a mixed one, both occur. Now, these are the exceptions mentioned for the periods previously ordained."

And so it is said in the *Saravali*:

> "If at the entry of a period a planet is strong or aspected by benefics, and is in the divisions of a benefic or a great friend, it will not cause death at that time. When the period of a weak lord of a sub-period occurs, that period becomes weak; then there is a cancellation of its effects and it certainly does not cause harm. If a planet is victorious in planetary war, is auspicious in its conjunction, and is situated in its exaltation and so on, there will be no suffering in its period."

This concludes verse 16.

**Vernacular Commentary:** Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious results of the planets mentioned above, a planet gives auspicious results in its auspicious period and inauspicious results in its inauspicious period. In a middling period, it gives mixed (both auspicious and inauspicious) results. This is because results follow the designation of the period. And the result of the Ascendant period is like that of the Lord of the Ascendant...

### Now, using the Shalini meter, the author explains how other results are also extended to the planetary periods:

**In the Chapter on Definitions:** For whichever planet a specific substance was mentioned—such as copper, gems, gold, etc.—the acquisition of that substance should be expected during its auspicious period <note>Dasha</note>. During an inauspicious period, there is loss of that substance. Similarly, whatever livelihood <term>Karmajiva: the means of earning a living</term> was instructed for a planet in the birth chart—such as wealth from the father, mother's family, etc.—that livelihood manifests specifically during that planet's sub-period. The author will later describe the effects of the houses, such as being "brave" or "stubborn," or "famous, clever, and a wanderer," or "having dim eyes in Aries," and so on. The effects of "aspects" refer to the results of planets looking at one another, such as "the Moon being aspected by a King or a Scholar." Regarding "combinations" <term>Yogas</term>: excluding the Celestial Combinations <term>Nabhasa Yogas</term>, among all other combinations, the strongest planet among those forming the yoga gives its result during its own period. The Celestial Combinations, however, give results throughout all periods. As will be stated: "Thus the Celestial Combinations have been described with their results; these should be considered as giving fixed results throughout all planetary periods." All such things mentioned should be applied without exception to that planet's period. ||20||

That is, when a planet's auspicious period occurs, there is gain of those substances and livelihoods, and during an inauspicious period, there is loss. ||20||

# Chapter on Planetary Periods and Sub-periods in the Brihat Jataka

### On the Radiance Created by the Great Elements

It was previously stated that the lords of the groups of Fire, Earth, Water, Air, and Ether are Mars and the other planets in their respective order. In this context, the Sun and the Moon are well known to represent Fire and Water. Any planet, upon reaching its own <term>Dasha</term><note>A major planetary period in a person's life</note>, manifests or reveals the <term>Chhaya</term><note>Literally "shadow," but here meaning "aura," "radiance," or "complexion"</note> created by the Great Elements. By the word **Chhaya**, the splendor of the body is meant; it signifies the luster of the physical form. Thus, it is commonly said, "This person possesses a good radiance" or "This person is devoid of radiance."

In this manner, during its own period, a planet reveals the bodily radiance produced by the Great Elements such as Earth. This radiance produces qualities born from the Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether. <insert>Earth is represented by 'Ku', Water by Varuna, Fire by the Consumer of Oblations, Air by Anila, and Ether by the Sky.</insert> These qualities are to be inferred, respectively, through the nose, mouth, eyes, skin, and ears.

*   **The Earthly quality** manifests as fragrance, inferred by the nose (the sense of smell).
*   **The Watery quality** manifests as taste, inferred by the mouth. <note>original: "Asya" (mouth)</note> By the word "mouth" here, the tongue should be understood, as that is how taste is perceived; the word "mouth" is used here to fit the poetic meter.
*   **The Fiery quality** manifests as form or color, inferred by the eyes.
*   **The Airy quality** manifests as the quality of touch, inferred by the skin.
*   **The Ethereal quality** manifests as sound, inferred by the ears.

The meaning is as follows:
When a person possesses a pleasant natural fragrance, it should be known as the **Earthly radiance** created by Mercury. When one enjoys sweet tastes, it is the **Watery radiance** created by the Moon and Venus. When a person is exceedingly handsome and of beautiful complexion, it is the **Fiery radiance** created by the Sun and Mars. When one is soft to the touch, it is the **Airy radiance** created by Saturn. When a person's speech is pleasing to the ears, it is the **Ethereal radiance** created by Jupiter.

The specific characteristics have been described by the Teacher in the *Samhita* <note>Referring to Varahamihira's other great work, the Brihat Samhita</note> as follows:

> "The radiance, which announces good and evil results, must be observed in humans, animals, and birds by those skilled in omens. It reveals the internal qualities of brilliance outwardly, like the light of a lamp residing within a vessel of crystal or gems.
>
> The radiance arising from **Earth** is characterized by glossy teeth, skin, nails, and hair, and a pleasant scent. It brings contentment, gain of wealth, and prosperity, and causes a daily increase in righteousness.
>
> The **Watery** radiance is glossy, white or greenish, and pleasing to the eyes. Like a mother, it brings about grace, softness, happiness, and the accomplishment of all goals for living beings.
>
> The **Fiery** radiance is fierce, bold, and has the color of a lotus, gold, or fire. It is endowed with brilliance, valor, and majesty. It leads to victory for living beings and quickly grants the fulfillment of desired objects.
>
> The radiance arising from **Air** is dirty, harsh, black, and has an evil smell. It produces imprisonment, bondage, disease, misfortune, and loss of wealth.
>
> The radiance arising from the **Sky (Ether)** is like crystal in appearance, extremely noble, and associated with good fortune. Like a hidden treasure, it is clear-colored and brings the highest blessings."

**Vernacular Commentary—** All planets, during their respective <term>Dasha</term><note>A major planetary period in Vedic astrology that governs a specific span of a person's life.</note>, manifest the "shadow" (the luster or complexion of the face and body) associated with their respective <term>Mahabhuta</term><note>The five great elements: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether.</note>. Furthermore, they manifest the qualities of Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether (namely: smell, taste, sight, touch, and sound) perceivable through the nose, mouth, eyes, and ears respectively, during their specific periods. ||21||

**Special Meaning—** The core idea is that the specific elements assigned to planets in the "Chapter on Definitions"—such as the verse beginning with <note>original: "shikhibhukhapayomarud"</note> "Fire, Earth, Ether, Water, and Air"—determine the luster of the limbs and the sensory qualities experienced during that planet's period. 

For example, the Sun and Mars belong to the Fire element. The "shadow" or manifestation of Fire is seen in the eyes, and its quality is sight (form). Therefore, during the auspicious <term>Dasha</term> or <term>Antardasha</term><note>A sub-period within a major planetary Dasha.</note> of the Sun or Mars, one experiences health in the eyes and happiness through beholding beautiful forms. 

Similarly, Mercury’s element is Earth; its manifestation is the beauty of the nose and its quality is smell. Thus, in Mercury's auspicious period, the nose remains healthy and beautiful, and one gains pleasure from fragrant substances. 

Jupiter’s element is Ether (Space); its manifestation is the luster of the ears and its quality is sound. Therefore, in Jupiter's auspicious period, the ears are healthy and one finds joy in hearing pleasant sounds; in an inauspicious period, there is ear disease and distress from harsh words. 

Venus and the Moon belong to the Water element; their manifestation is the mouth (and tongue) and their quality is taste. Thus, in the auspicious periods of Venus and the Moon, the mouth remains clean and one enjoys various delicious foods. In an inauspicious period, there are mouth diseases and distress from poor-tasting food. 

Finally, Saturn’s element is Air; its quality is touch and its manifestation is the luster of the skin. Therefore, during Saturn's period, the skin's beauty increases and one finds happiness through excellent touch (such as garlands, fine silk garments, ornaments, or the company of a young woman). In an inauspicious period, one suffers from skin diseases and painful touch (such as wounds from weapons). 

Therefore, for those whose birth charts are available, one should predict these results by understanding the planetary periods. For those whose birth time is unknown, one should infer the current planetary period based on the manifestation of these results. This is what the author explains in the following verse. ||21||

*Now, except for the "Airy" shadow, auspicious and inauspicious results have been described for all shadows. How is this? To understand how one recognizes "this is an auspicious result" or "this is an inauspicious result," the author describes the state of the inner soul (Antaratma) through its purity or impurity—*

> ->During the period of a planet giving auspicious results, the inner soul becomes likewise,<-
> ->bringing great happiness and the arrival of wealth to men.<-
> ->By observing the ripening of these described results, one should infer the current period;<-
> ->the prediction of results is refined through dreams, thoughts, and one's own strength. ||22||<-

# Chapter on Planetary Periods and Sub-periods

### Page 216
-> From the *Brihat Jataka* <-

**"Giving auspicious results..."** <note>original: *shubhaphalada*</note> This refers to a planet that bestows favorable outcomes. During the major period <term>Dasha; the primary time-block in a person's life ruled by a specific planet</term> of such an auspicious planet, the inner self <note>original: *antaratma*; the soul or inner consciousness</note> residing within the body becomes similarly auspicious and takes on the nature of pure consciousness. During the time indicated by that planet's period, the person's "shadow" <note>original: *chhaya*; here referring to the aura or reflected physical vitality</note> produces many kinds of happiness, a sense of well-being, and the arrival of wealth.

Conversely, during an inauspicious period, the person's inner self also becomes inauspicious. In that state, the shadow produced by that planet gives results accordingly, generating unhappiness and the arrival of misfortunes of many kinds. In a mixed period, the results are mixed. Regarding travel <note>referring to *Yatra*, the branch of astrology dealing with expeditions</note>, it is said:

> "The subtle radiance residing in the body, which follows omens and is 
> greater than the senses, expands into the results of the three periods of 
> time <note>past, present, and future</note>. When the mind is not at 
> peace, it does not rejoice even in success. Therefore, the state of the 
> traveler's mind should be inferred by all means. All omens, good and 
> bad, are on one side; on the other side is the purity of the mind. 
> Purity of mind brings victory."

**"By the ripening of the stated results..."** <note>original: *kathitaphalavipakair*</note> The auspicious or inauspicious results described for the planetary periods are experienced by a person; by observing these, one should understand which planet's period is currently active. This means: whatever kind of result—good or bad—is being experienced by a person, one should look up which planet's period that result is attributed to. One should then conclude or "infer" that such a period is currently in progress for that man. Thus, by means of the "shadow," the state of the inner self, or the ripening of results, one should declare the current period of the calculated horoscope.

Now, it was mentioned that in an inauspicious Saturnian period <note>original: *sauradasha*</note>, there is a loss of limbs, but this is not said for an auspicious one. However, even in inauspicious periods, the loss of limbs is seen in many cases. In an auspicious Venusian period, the finding of treasure is mentioned, yet that is not always seen. To explain this, the text says: **"The statement of results transforms..."** <note>original: *parinamati phaloktir*</note>. When results—whether good or bad—are given by planets that are weak <note>original: *aviryaih*; lacking strength in the birth chart</note>, the fulfillment of those results is experienced only in a dream state <note>original: *svapnavastha*</note>, or merely as a worry or a mental desire.

Some scholars read the text as: "In an auspicious period, the sub-period is named likewise." They explain it this way: if the sub-period <term>Antardasha; a secondary period within the major Dasha</term> within an auspicious major period is also auspicious, then it produces great happiness and wealth for men. If the sub-period within an inauspicious major period is inauspicious, it produces much unhappiness and misfortune. 

However, this interpretation does not account for mixed results where an inauspicious sub-period occurs within an auspicious major period. As it is stated elsewhere: "The lord of the sub-period, occupying the same sign, takes half the power and gives its own result." Otherwise, the word "takes" would be meaningless. Therefore, the first reading <note>focusing on the inner state/shadow</note> is superior; the second is a mistaken reading. Without the first reading, it is impossible to infer the auspicious or inauspicious nature of a period through the "shadow." // 22 //

**Vernacular Translation—** During the period <note>Dasha: a specific span of time in a person's life ruled by a particular planet</note> of a beneficial planet, the Inner Soul (the God residing within one's heart) becomes favorable and grants humans all types of happiness and financial gain. "Now, the method for understanding the planetary periods of one whose birth time is unknown is described"—one should estimate the current planetary period based on the specific results and effects that have been attributed to each planet. Furthermore, if a planet is weak <term>Nirbal: lacking in positional or directional strength</term>, the results of its period (whether good or bad) are experienced only in dreams or in one's thoughts and desires. ||22||

For example, if someone is currently receiving excellent food every day, one should infer that since taste is a quality of water and water is the element of Venus, the period of Venus is currently active. Similarly, suppose someone is undergoing the "descending" period <term>Avarohini: a period where a planet's influence is waning or moving toward debilitation</term> of a malefic planet situated in an enemy's sign; if that planet is strong, the person will suffer total loss and distress. If, during that time, a "rising" <term>Arohini: a period where a planet's influence is increasing or moving toward exaltation</term> sub-period <note>Antardasha: a minor cycle within a major planetary period</note> of a planet in a favorable position occurs, but that planet is weak, the person will experience the happiness promised by that sub-period only in dreams or through wishful thinking.

There is an illustrative story: a man was under the influence of a powerful, inauspicious planetary period, so despite his best efforts, he could not obtain wealth or happiness. Eventually, a one-month sub-period of a weak but beneficial planet arrived. A merchant hired him to deliver a pot of ghee <note>Ghruta: clarified butter, a valuable commodity</note> from one place to another for a daily wage of 8 annas <note>An anna was a currency unit formerly used in India, equal to 1/16th of a rupee</note>. He started the work with great joy. While carrying the pot of ghee on his head, he began to think: "I will earn eight annas in wages. I will spend four annas on rice, lentils, and vegetables to eat my fill, and I will save four annas every day. In one month, I will save seven and a half rupees. Even if the work ends, I will start a business with that money; I have heard people become millionaires starting with just one rupee. Surely I can become a 'thousand-aire' with seven rupees! Then, with even more money saved, I will buy a horse, put a saddle on it, and ride like this—" 

Just as he thought this, he jumped with excitement, and the pot of ghee fell from his head and shattered. He lost even his single day's wages. Because the ruler of the sub-period was weak and the ruler of the major period was strong, the major planet did not allow him to gain physical happiness or wealth. He only experienced the joy and financial gain in his mind until the sub-period of the weak, beneficial planet ended. ||22||

# Page 218
## Chapter on Planetary Periods and Sub-periods in the Brihat Jataka

Now, the author explains through a verse in the *Vasantatilaka* meter how two similar but opposing effects given by a single planet cancel each other out, whereas effects given by different planets simply manifest in their respective turns.

**If a single planet yields two similar but contradictory results,**
**one should declare their destruction; however, if one effect is more powerful, that one comes to fruition.**
**A different planet does not destroy the similar result of another;**
**rather, each planet gives its own specific result when its own period arrives. || 23 ||**

->Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Planetary Periods and Sub-periods,"<-
->in the Brihat Jataka composed by the Great Teacher Varāhamihira.<- <note>Note 1: See the end of the book for a clearer explanation of periods and sub-periods.</note>

**Commentary:** Regarding the phrase "of a single planet": It has been stated that a planet gives all its results during its period (except for those results pertaining to the *Nabhasa* <term>Nabhasa: specific celestial yoga configurations</term> combinations). In a situation where a single planet gives two results that are dissimilar and contradictory, if those two results are of equal strength (similar), one should declare the "destruction" or cancellation of those results. 

What constitutes such a contradiction? For example: suppose a planet, by some logic of its period-effect, is a "giver of gold" <note>original: "suvarṇada"</note>. Yet, by another logic—such as its strength in the *Ashtakavarga* <term>Ashtakavarga: a mathematical system of points used to calculate planetary strength</term>, its planetary combinations, its aspects, or its house position—that same planet becomes a "stealer of gold" <note>original: "suvarṇāpahārī"</note>. In this case, both effects relate to gold (the similarity), but one gives and the other takes (the contradiction). Therefore, one should predict a cancellation: there is neither a gain of gold nor a loss.

"If one is more powerful, that one comes to fruition": If two different results are given by the same planet, the stronger one prevails. For instance, if a planet is a "giver of gold" for two reasons but a "stealer of gold" for only one reason, then because the giving is more frequent/powerful, it will indeed give gold and not take it away. Alternatively, if it is a stealer for two reasons and a giver for one, it will take it away. Some also argue that if a planet is a stealer of gold but a giver of silver, these are dissimilar; because they are dissimilar, the more prominent one manifests, or both manifest in their own way.

"A different planet does not...": A result given by one planet is not destroyed or cancelled by another planet, even if the results are contradictory. For example, if one planet is a giver of gold and another is a stealer of gold, the giver will provide gold during its own period, and the stealer will take it away during its own period. By this, it is meant that while a single planet's contradictory effects might cancel out across the entire lifespan, the effects of different planets do not cancel; they simply wait for their respective periods. A planet that has reached its own period <term>Dasha: the major time-block assigned to a specific planet</term> will produce the gain of gold, while the stealer...

<insert>(1) A detailed clarification of periods and sub-periods should be clearly looked for at the end of the volume.</insert>

When a planet reaches its own period (<term>Dasha</term>: a specific time block in a person's life ruled by a planet), it takes away gold <note>This likely refers to the loss of wealth or specific material effects mentioned in the preceding verse</note>. Regarding the results of the <term>Ashtakavarga</term> (a system of points used to predict planetary strength), if a single planet produces both auspicious and inauspicious results of equal number, they cancel each other out. How this destruction of results occurs will be explained in that specific section. // 23 //

->Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Periods and Sub-periods,"<-
->in the Commentary on the Brihat Jataka composed by Shri Bhattotpala.<-

**Vernacular Translation (Hindi)**— If the auspicious and inauspicious strengths of a single planet are equal, then both results are destroyed; that is, the planet yields neither good nor bad results. If there is an imbalance, the result that is greater will prevail. However, one planet does not destroy the opposing results of a *different* planet; rather, each planet gives its own specific result during its own period. // 23 //

**Special Note**— The deeper meaning is this: if a single planet, according to the <term>Shadvarga</term> (six-fold division of a sign), falls into 3 auspicious divisions and 3 inauspicious divisions, the results cancel out due to equality. If it is in 4 auspicious and 2 inauspicious divisions, it will give a good result because the good is greater, but one should understand it will only give one-third of the total potential good. A planet in only auspicious divisions gives full results. However, if in any birth chart 3 separate planets are auspicious and 3 are inauspicious, they do not cancel each other out because they are different entities. Each will give its own result during its respective period. // 23 //

# Chapter 9: The Ashtakavarga (Eight-fold Division)

Now the chapter on <term>Ashtakavarga</term> is explained. The results of sub-periods were stated previously; now is the opportunity for the fixed results of the Ashtakavarga. All planets, including the Ascendant (<term>Lagna</term>), are considered. From their positions, the auspicious and inauspicious results of each individual planet as it moves through the signs (<term>Gocharas</term> or transits) are described in the Ashtakavarga. First, the author describes the Ashtakavarga of the Sun (<term>Arka</term>) in the *Shardulavikridita* meter:

> From his own position, the Sun is auspicious in the 1st, 11th, 4th, 8th, 2nd, 10th, 9th, and 7th houses.
> From Mars, he is the same as from his own position. From Saturn, the same. From Venus, in the 7th, 6th, and 12th.
> From Jupiter, in the 5th, 11th, 6th, and 9th. From the Moon, in the 10th, 3rd, and 11th.
> From Mercury, in the 12th, 5th, 6th, 9th, 10th, and 11th. From the Ascendant, in the 3rd, 4th, 6th, 10th, 11th, and 12th. // 1 //

**"From his own position..."** The sign in which the Sun was located at the time of a person's birth is called its "own place" (<term>Svasthana</term>). This should be understood for all other planets as well. Wherever a planet is situated is its own place. From that spot, the Sun is auspicious in the 1st, 11th, 4th, 8th, 2nd, 10th, 9th...

In the seventh [house] 1, 11, 4, 8, 2, 10, 6, 7 <note>These numbers refer to specific houses or positions relative to a planet</note> the names of these places have been explained previously. The Sun, when moving through these places from its own position, is auspicious and gives desired results. However, in other places, it is inauspicious and gives undesired results. As it will be said: "This is declared as desirable; the rest is not desirable"—this is how it should be understood everywhere. Just as from its own position, it is auspicious from Mars <note>original: "vakra," a name for Mars meaning "the crooked/retrograde one"</note>. In the same places as from its own position—1, 11, 4, 8, 2, 10, 6, 7—the Sun is auspicious from Mars. Likewise from the son of the Sun <note>Saturn</note>. In the same places where it is auspicious from itself, it is also from Saturn: 1, 11, 4, 8, 2, 10, 6, 7. In these, the Sun is auspicious from Saturn; the word "auspicious" follows through the whole context. From Venus, in the seventh, twelfth, and sixth houses, that same Sun is auspicious: 7, 12, 6. From Mercury, it is auspicious in these same places as well as the "end," "penance," and "son" houses. In these previously mentioned Moon positions (10, 3, 11) and the word "and" implies the end, penance, and son houses from Mercury: 10, 3, 11, 6, 12, 9, 5. From the Ascendant <note>Lagna</note>, it moves in the "joint" and "end" along with the previously mentioned Moon positions which are drawn forward; by this, the "end, penance, and son" positions are the general definition everywhere. Therefore, in these Moon positions of 10, 3, 11, 6, along with the "joint" and "end" (the fourth and twelfth), the Sun is auspicious from the Ascendant: 10, 3, 11, 6, 4, 12.

"From Jupiter"—from the Guru's position, in the 12th, 11th, 8th, and the angles: 12, 11, 8, 1, 4, 7, 10. "From Venus"—from the position of Venus, in the 9th, 4th...

# Page 223
## Commentary by Bhattotpala on the Language of the Stars

->**Mars in the Upachaya houses from the Sun, etc.**<-

**Mars** <note>original: "Vakra" - the twisted or retrograde one, a common name for Mars</note> is auspicious when situated in the **Upachaya** <note>The 3rd, 6th, 10th, and 11th houses, associated with growth and improvement</note> houses—namely the third, sixth, eleventh, and tenth—along with the house of the son <note>the 5th house</note> from the **Sun** <note>original: "Ina"</note>. The numerical positions are 3, 6, 11, 10, and 5. From the **Ascendant** <note>original: "Udaya" or "Lagna"</note>, Mars is auspicious in these same Upachaya houses plus the first house <note>the self/body</note>: 3, 6, 11, 10, and 1. From the **Moon**, it is auspicious in these Upachaya houses except for the tenth, where it is "fruitless" <note>original: "digviphaleshu"</note>, meaning in the tenth house it produces neither good nor bad results. Thus, from the Moon, the auspicious positions are 3, 6, and 11.

From **its own position** <note>Mars' position in the birth chart</note>, it is auspicious when moving through the angles <note>1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</note>, the house of death <note>8th</note>, the house of gains <note>11th</note>, and the house of wealth <note>2nd</note>: 1, 4, 7, 10, 8, 11, and 2. From **Saturn** <note>original: "Arkatanaya" - son of the Sun</note>, it is auspicious in the ninth, eleventh, eighth, and the angles: 9, 11, 8, 1, 4, 7, and 10. From **Mercury** <note>original: "Jna"</note>, it is auspicious in the sixth, third, fifth, and eleventh: 6, 3, 5, and 11.

From **Venus**, it is auspicious in the sixth, twelfth, eleventh, and eighth: 6, 12, 11, and 8. From **Jupiter** <note>original: "Guru" or "Jiva"</note>, it is auspicious in the tenth, twelfth, eleventh, and sixth: 10, 12, 11, and 6.

As **Satyacharya** <note>An ancient authority on astrology</note> says: "Excluding the twelfth, fifth, ninth, third, and sixth, Mars is auspicious from its own place." By excluding these, we arrive at the same positions taught by **Varahamihira**: 1, 4, 7, 10, 8, 11, and 2. Regarding Saturn, excluding the second house but including the ninth, the positions are 11, 8, 6, 1, 4, and 10.

Mars is desired in the 3rd, 5th, 10th, 11th, and 6th from the **Sun**. From the **Moon**, it is neutral in the 10th, but auspicious in 3, 6, and 11. Mars is honored in the 10th, 11th, 6th, and 12th from **Jupiter's** position. From **Mercury**, Mars is auspicious in the 6th, 11th, 5th, and 3rd. From **Venus**, it is honored in the 12th, 11th, 8th, and 6th. From the **Ascendant**, it is auspicious in the 1st, 11th, 10th, 6th, and 3rd.

As stated in the **Svalpajataka**:
"Mars is auspicious in its own house, the house of gains, and the angles from itself; in the 11th, 6th, and 5th from Mercury; in the 10th, 11th, 6th, and 12th from Jupiter; and in the Upachaya houses and the 5th from the Sun. From the Ascendant, it is auspicious in the Upachayas and the first house. From the Moon, it is auspicious in the Upachayas except the tenth, where it is neutral." <note>The text emphasizes that in the 10th from the Moon, it is specifically not "auspicious" but neutral.</note> From **Venus**, it is in the 12th, 6th, 8th, and 11th. From **Saturn**, it is in the angles, the 11th, 9th, 6th, and 8th.

**This concludes the Ashtakavarga of Mars.**

In these very places previously mentioned starting from the **Sun**, with the addition of the third and ninth houses, Jupiter is auspicious: 10, 2, 9, 8, 7, 11, 4, 3, 6. <note>The text lists the numerical houses from the Sun where Jupiter provides positive results.</note> From **Venus** (Bhargava), he is auspicious in the fifth, second, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and sixth houses: 5, 2, 9, 10, 11, 6. From the **Moon** (Himago), he is auspicious in the seventh, eleventh, second, ninth, and fifth houses: 7, 11, 2, 9, 5. From **Saturn** (Manda), he is auspicious in the third, sixth, fifth, and twelfth houses: 3, 6, 5, 12. From **Mercury** (Gna), he is auspicious in the tenth, fifth, sixth, second, fourth, eleventh, first, and ninth houses: 10, 5, 6, 2, 4, 11, 1, 9. From the **Ascendant** (Udaya), he is auspicious in these same places with the addition of the seventh house: 10, 5, 6, 2, 4, 11, 1, 9, 7.

And so says **Satyacharya**: <note>An ancient authority on astrology often cited by Varahamihira.</note> "In those places where the Moon is auspicious for Mercury, Jupiter is abundant from his own position." The Ashtakavarga of the Moon is now recited. Excluding the sixth, second, ninth, and twelfth houses, he is praised from Mercury: 6, 2, 9, 12. <note>original: "पश्चिमो" (paschimo) refers to the 12th house.</note> Excluding these places, the remaining are: 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11.

Here, regarding the fifth and second houses, there is a difference of opinion with **Varahamihira**. <note>The author of the Brihat Jataka.</note> In this instance, Varahamihira, accepting the opinion of **Yavanesvara**, <note>Literally "Lord of the Greeks," referring to early Indo-Greek astrological authorities.</note> has accepted the auspiciousness of the second house. As Yavanesvara says: "From his own position, Jupiter in the second house brings gain of position, children, wealth, and honor." Thus, he is auspicious in the second. However, due to "dispute, poverty, and travel," he is not auspicious in the fifth house (the trine).

From the **Sun** and others, he is desired in these houses, with the addition of the ninth: 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. Here also, regarding the fifth and second houses, Varahamihira accepted Yavanesvara's view. As Yavanesvara says: "In the Sun's place, Jupiter in the second house bestows intelligence, friends, and wealth." Because of this auspiciousness, Varahamihira accepted it. Since "Jupiter causes sickness, royal displeasure, and travel" in the fifth, he is not auspicious in the fifth.

From **Mars** (Kuja), Jupiter is indicated in similar places, excluding the house of siblings (the 3rd): 1, 4, 5, 7, 10, 11. Here too, there is a difference with Varahamihira regarding the fifth and second houses. Here again, Yavanesvara says: "Jupiter situated in Mars's place is a destroyer of enemies, and in the second, he is a giver of great joy." Therefore, Varahamihira accepted the second house. Being in the seventh (Jamitra) causes disease, enemies, and grief; thus, the seventh house is not accepted.

From **Saturn**, he is auspicious in the twelfth, sixth, fifth, and third: 12, 6, 5, 3. From **Venus** (Bhrigu), in the tenth, eleventh, ninth, second, sixth, and fifth: 10, 11, 9, 2, 6, 5. From the **Moon**, Jupiter is auspicious in the seventh, ninth, fifth, eleventh, and second: 7, 9, 5, 11, 2. From **Mercury** (Saumya), Jupiter is indicated in the first, second, fifth, fourth, ninth, sixth, eleventh, and tenth: 1, 2, 5...
