# Chapter on Nabhasa Yogas in the Brihat Jataka
### Page 260

Since the Moon can be considered either a benefic <note>auspicious</note> or a malefic <note>inauspicious</note> depending on whether it is the waxing or waning fortnight, a question arises: if the Moon is waning and occupies the fourth center <term>Kendra: the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses of a birth chart</term> while the other three centers are occupied by benefics, or similarly by malefics, do the "Garland" (Srak) and "Serpent" (Sarpa) combinations still form? Why was this not explicitly detailed for all four centers? It is explained thus: In the *Svalpa Jataka*, it is stated, "With the three centers occupied by malefics, it is called the 'Half-Wheel' (Dala) group, specifically the Serpent; otherwise, the Garland." How do we know there are only three planets involved? Because the Moon is not counted as the third among them in these specific instances. As the Sage Garga said: "When Saturn, Mars, and the Sun occupy three centers, the Serpent yoga is formed, giving birth to one who is miserable. The Garland yoga, giving birth to one who enjoys life, is formed similarly by Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury." <note>original: "त्रिकेन्द्रगैर्यमारार्कैः..."</note>

How is it determined that the Garland yoga exists when centers are free of malefics, and the Serpent when free of benefics? It is said by Badarayana: "When Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter are in three centers without malefics, they call it Garland. But when the non-benefics—Saturn, Mars, and the Sun—are so placed, it is the Serpent. These two are known as the Dala (Half-Wheel) yogas." These two Dala yogas, Garland and Serpent, were taught by Parasara. Though some claim others did not mention them, Varahamihira included them in his own treatise because Parasara taught them. Likewise, Manittha says: "With malefics or benefics in three centers, the two yogas called Serpent and Garland are formed, yielding destroyed or desired fruits respectively." Thus, the three "Asraya" (Refuge) yogas were mentioned by some and not by others; because they were taught by ancient authorities, Varahamihira collected them in this science. Thus, the two Dala yogas are explained. || 2 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** If all planets are in Moveable signs, it is *Rajju* (Rope) yoga; if all are in Fixed signs, it is *Musala* (Pestle) yoga; and if all are in Dual-natured signs, it is *Nala* (Reed) yoga. Satyacharya calls these three the "Refuge" (Asraya) yogas. Furthermore, if the benefic planets (Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—these three) are in three centers, these two types of Dala yogas occur. Parasara named these Dala yogas "Garland" (Mala) and "Serpent" (Sarpa) respectively. That is, if the centers are joined by benefics, it is Garland; if joined by malefics, it is Serpent. || 2 ||

**Special Meaning:** Regarding the Moveable signs and others, some interpret this to mean all four Moveable, all four Fixed, or all four Dual signs must be occupied. However, that contradicts the words of the Sages. As the Sage Garga said: "Whether in one, two, three, or all, when Moveable signs are joined by planets, 
->then the Moveable yoga called Rajju is formed, giving birth to those who wander." etc.<- 
Furthermore, in the Dala yoga, the Moon is excluded because it is considered distinct from both pure benefics and pure malefics; this is because the Moon does not possess inherent beneficence at all times. It acquires maleficence through association with malefics. As is the word of the Sage Garga:

> "When Saturn, Mars, and the Sun occupy three centers, the Serpent yoga is formed, giving birth to one who is miserable. The Garland yoga, giving birth to one who enjoys life, is formed similarly by Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury."

## With the Sanskrit Commentary of Bhattotpala and Hindi Translation

As per Badarayana <note>An ancient sage and authority on astrology</note>—here too, the Dala Yoga occurs only when either exclusively benefic or exclusively malefic planets occupy the angles (Kendras).

->'When the benefics Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter occupy three of the angles,<-
->they call it the Mala (Garland) Yoga.<-
->When the malefics Saturn, Mars, and the Sun occupy three angles,<-
->it is Sarpa (Serpent) Yoga; these two are called the Dala Yogas.' || 2 ||<-

Now, the author explains in the Upajati meter why other teachers have described the three Ashraya Yogas and the two Dala Yogas in a different manner:

->'The Ashraya Yogas attain equality with the<-
->Yava, Abja, Vajra, Andaja, and Golaka Yogas.<-
->Others say the Dala Yogas yield the results already described<-
->for planets in angles, and do not have separate results.' || 3 ||<-

**The Ashraya Yogas...** The combinations known as Ashraya Yogas—namely Rajju, Mushala, and Nala—attain "equality" or similarity with the Akriti (Shape) Yogas such as Yava (Barley), Padma (Lotus), Vajra (Thunderbolt), Vihanga (Bird), and Golaka (Globe). By the word "etcetera," this includes Gada (Mace) and Shakata (Wagon), as well as the Sankhya (Numerical) Yogas like Gola, Yuga, Shula, and Kedara. Because these Ashraya Yogas are often subsumed within these other categories, some teachers do not mention them separately. However, Varahamihira <note>The 6th-century author of this text, the Brihat Jataka</note> has mentioned them because there are instances where Ashraya Yogas can exist independently. We shall explain at the end of this chapter where these do not overlap.

**Regarding the Dala Yogas...** It is said that the two Dala Yogas yield the "results already described" for planets situated in the angles (Kendras). The results for benefics in three angles are auspicious, and for malefics, they are inauspicious. This is why they are called "described results." As Varahamihira himself stated:

> 'Benefics in the angles and trines are praised; in those same places, malefics do not grant auspicious results.'

Because it is already known that benefics in the angles/trines produce good results, the Mala Yoga was not specifically detailed as a separate result by some. Similarly, because malefics in three angles produce bad results, the Sarpa Yoga was not separately detailed. Thus, "others say" they do not have "separate results" because the meaning is already implied.

If that is the case, why did Varahamihira mention them? It is said here: because they are included among the <term>Nabhasa Yogas</term> <note>Celestial combinations that are said to affect a person throughout their entire life, rather than just during specific planetary periods</note>, they give results throughout all the <term>Dashas</term> <note>Planetary life-cycles or periods</note>. When the results of planets in angles are considered without a specific "Yoga" formation, they only give results during their own specific periods. This follows the opinion of Parashara and others. In their view, as Nabhasa Yogas, these two provide results in all periods; therefore, Varahamihira included them. || 3 ||

**Hindi Translation—** These three Ashraya Yogas are similar to the Yava, Kamala, Vajra, Vihaga, Gola, and other Yogas which will be described later (meaning they possess the same characteristics...

# Chapter on Nabhasa Yogas in the Brihat Jataka

...because of being [included within those same yogas]. Furthermore, other teachers have stated that the two *Dala* <note>literally "petal" or "group" yogas</note> yogas, which are formed by having benefic or malefic planets in the *Kendras* <term>Kendra: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses of a birth chart, considered the pillars of strength</term>, do not give results different from the *Yava* and other similar yogas. || 3 ||

**Special Meaning—** If other teachers did not mention the *Ashraya* and *Dala* yogas, why did Varahamihira <note>The 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath who authored this text</note> include them? He will explain the reason for this himself later on. || 3 ||

Now, he describes five *Akriti* <note>shape-based</note> yogas named Gada, Shakata, Vihaga, Shringataka, and Hala in the *Vasantatilaka* meter:

->**When all planets occupy two adjacent angular houses, it is Gada.**<-
->**When in the first and seventh, it is Shakata; in the tenth and fourth, Vihaga.**<-
->**When all planets are situated in the ninth, fifth, and the first, it is Shringataka.**<-
->**When in other triangular houses excluding the first, the experts call it Hala. || 4 ||**<-

**Commentary:** "Adjacent" means nearby. When all planets are in a pair of adjacent *Kendra* houses (angular signs), the yoga is called *Gada* <note>meaning "Mace" or "Club"</note>. This is of four types: 1. All planets in the 1st and 4th houses. 2. In the 4th and 7th. 3. In the 7th and 10th. 4. In the 10th and 1st. "In the body and setting" means when all planets are in the 1st (Ascendant) and 7th houses, it is *Shakata* <note>meaning "Wagon" or "Cart"</note>. When all planets are in the 10th and 4th houses, it is the yoga called *Vihaga* <note>meaning "Bird"</note>. When all planets are in the 9th, 5th, and 1st houses, it is the *Shringataka* <note>meaning "Horned" or "Triangle"</note> yoga. "In others, it is Hala" means that excluding the 1st house, if all planets are placed in mutual *Trikona* <term>Trikona: Trine houses, specifically the 1st, 5th, and 9th, or any series of houses 120 degrees apart</term> positions, the experts of *Hora Shastra* <note>Astrology</note> call it *Hala* <note>meaning "Plough"</note>. This is of three types: 1. All planets in the 2nd, 6th, and 10th houses. 2. In the 3rd, 7th, and 11th. 3. In the 4th, 8th, and 12th houses. || 4 ||

**Translation:** If all planets are placed in two adjacent *Kendras* (such as 1st-4th, 4th-7th, 7th-10th, 10th-1st), the yoga is named *Gada*. If all planets are in the 1st and 7th, it is *Shakata*, and if all planets are in the 10th and 4th, it is *Vihaga* (Bird) yoga. If all planets are in the 1st, 5th, and 9th (the trines), it is *Shringataka* yoga. Similarly, if all planets fall in mutual trines starting from a house other than the 1st (such as starting from the 2nd or 3rd), it is called *Hala* yoga. || 4 ||

**Special Meaning—** Regarding the placement of planets in two adjacent *Kendras*, the ancient *Yavanacharyas* <note>literally "Greek Teachers," referring to the transmission of Hellenistic astrology to India</note> described four distinct names for these four yogas. For example: (1) *Gada* in the 1st-4th; (2) *Shankha* (Conch) in the 4th-7th; (3) *Vabhru* (Mongoose) in the 7th-10th; and (4) *Dhvaja* (Banner) if all planets are in the 10th-1st. Therefore, in their opinion, there are 23 *Akriti* yogas. Varahamihira has grouped all four of these under the single name 'Gada'; thus, in his system, there are 20 *Akriti* yogas. || 4 ||

# Commentary on the Language of Bhattotpala
## Page 263

Now, he describes four planetary combinations <note>Yogas</note> named Diamond <note>Vajra</note>, Barley <note>Yava</note>, Lotus <note>Kamala</note>, and Pond <note>Vapi</note> in the *Vaitaliya* meter:

**If the benefics and malefics are placed like the Cart and Bird combinations, it is Diamond; if reversed, it is Barley.**
**If they are mixed, it is Lotus; if they are outside the angles, it is Pond. || 5 ||**

Regarding "Cart and Bird" <note>Shakata and Andaja</note>: If the benefics are arranged like the Cart <note>in the 1st and 7th houses</note> and the malefics like the Bird <note>in the 4th and 10th houses</note>, the **Diamond** <note>Vajra</note> yoga occurs. This means: benefics are in the Ascendant and the 7th house, and malefics are in the 4th and 10th houses, with no planets elsewhere. If these same planets are reversed, it is the **Barley** <note>Yava</note> yoga. That is, malefics like the Cart and benefics like the Bird. To clarify: malefics situated in the Ascendant and 7th, and benefics in the 4th and 10th, create the Barley yoga.

Regarding **Lotus** <note>Kamala</note>: If these same benefics and malefics are mixed together and situated across all four angles <note>Kendras: 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</note>, the Lotus yoga occurs. If that same Lotus configuration occurs outside of the angles, it is called the **Pond** <note>Vapi</note> yoga. This means: when all planets are placed outside the angles—avoiding the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th—and are instead in the succeedent <term>Panaphara<gloss>houses 2, 5, 8, 11</gloss></term> or cadent <term>Apoklima<gloss>houses 3, 6, 9, 12</gloss></term> houses, that Lotus-like arrangement is called Pond yoga. This applies if they are in the four succeedent or the four cadent houses. || 5 ||

---

**Vernacular Translation—** Here, Varahamihira’s intention is: if all benefic planets are like the Cart (in the Ascendant and 7th) and all malefic planets are like the Bird (in the 10th and 4th), it is **Diamond Yoga**. Conversely, if all malefics are in the Ascendant/7th and all benefics are in the 10th/4th, it is **Barley Yoga**. If both malefics and benefics are mixed within the angles, it is **Lotus Yoga**. If all mixed planets are in places other than the angles (meaning all in succeedent or all in cadent houses), then in both cases it is called **Pond Yoga**. || 5 ||

*Special Interpretation—* In this regard, Varahamihira’s intended meaning seems inconsistent <note>original: "asangat"</note>, as he himself reveals in a later verse. Therefore, if an alternative interpretation is taken here, the statements of the ancient teachers and Varahamihira become consistent. For example:

Sanskrit Commentary— *'If benefics are like the Cart and malefics are like the Bird, it is Diamond Yoga; if situated the opposite way, it is Barley.'*

**Vernacular Translation—** Like the Cart (all benefics in the 1st/7th OR all malefics in the 4th/10th is Diamond Yoga) and the opposite (all malefics in the 1st/7th OR all benefics in the 4th/10th is Barley Yoga). This is how the meaning is specified.

They give their auspicious results in the later stages of life (old age). The shape of Indra's thunderbolt <note>Vajra</note> is such that both its ends (the base and the tip) possess equal power. Therefore, because it gives results at the beginning and the end of life, it is named **Vajra**.

(2) Similarly, when all benefic planets are situated in the middle quadrants (the 10th and 4th houses), the auspicious results occur only in the middle age, and not at the beginning or the end. -> Now, the Vajra and Yava yogas are not actually possible here, but I have <-
-> described them according to the ancient scriptures; he states this in an Anushtubh verse: <-

# I have described the Vajra and other yogas following the ancient scriptures.
# How can Mercury and Venus [1] ever be in the fourth house from the Sun? || 6 ||

"Following the ancient scriptures": According to the ancient scriptures and the previous teachers such as Maya, Yavana, and others, the yoga called **Vajra** and the yoga called **Yava** were established. Therefore, I have also included them. The use of the plural "Vajra and others" is intended to show other yogas of this type. Even if these yogas [seemingly] occur, I have recorded them following the ancient scriptures. This means I have included them after observing and following those texts. Because, from the Sun, in the fourth house or fourth sign, whether ahead or behind—

> [1] <margin>By the previously mentioned rule, "If all planets are in the 1st and 7th houses, it is Shakata; if in the 4th and 10th, it is Vihaga," we understand the structure. Furthermore, "Vajra is formed like Shakata and Vihaga but with benefics and malefic reversed; Yava is the opposite of that." By this statement, if benefic planets are in the 1st and 7th houses while malefic planets are in the 4th and 10th, the **Vajra** yoga is formed. Conversely, if all malefic planets are in the 1st and 7th and all benefics are in the 4th and 10th, the **Yava** yoga was described by ancient teachers. However, such yogas are impossible. When the Sun is in the Ascendant (1st), Mercury and Venus cannot possibly be in the 4th or 10th houses. Similarly, if the Sun is in the 4th, Mercury and Venus can never be in the 1st or 7th. This is because the mean positions of Mercury and Venus are always equal to the mean Sun. The maximum distance between the calculated Sun and Mercury, or the Sun and Venus, can never exceed one zodiac sign (30 degrees). If we take the maximum negative equation of the Sun and the maximum positive equations of Mercury/Venus, or vice versa, the maximum possible separation according to mathematical methods <term>Ganita-riti: astronomical calculation</term> is as follows: Sun's max equation is 2° 9' 39"; Mercury's combined max equations are 27° 33' 37". Added together, this is 29° 44' 08", which is less than one full sign. Therefore, Mercury can only be separated from the true Sun by slightly less than one sign, either ahead or behind. The same should be understood for Venus. Therefore, since Mercury and Venus cannot be in the fourth house from the Sun, the Vajra and Yava yogas are logically impossible.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of planetary combinations (Yogas) and addresses a mathematical impossibility found in earlier astrological texts regarding the positions of Mercury and Venus relative to the Sun.</meta>

<page-num>265</page-num>
<header>Page 265, including Bhattotpala's Sanskrit Commentary and the Hindi Translation</header>

How can Mercury and Venus be so positioned? Never at sunrise or sunset, nor at midday or midnight, are Mercury and Venus found in such places. When the Sun is at the meridian <note>midday</note> or at the midnight point, their rising or setting simply does not occur in that manner. || 6 ||

**Vernacular Translation—** Having observed the works of ancient teachers like Maya, Yavana, and Manittha, I too have described the characteristics of the *Vajra* <note>Thunderbolt</note> and other Yogas. In reality—in the *Vajra* and *Yava* <note>Barley-corn</note> Yogas, Mercury and Venus are placed in the fourth house from the Sun; how can this be possible? That is to say, this type of combination can never actually occur. || 6 ||

**Special Meaning—** Varahamihira <note>The famous 6th-century Indian astronomer</note>, in describing the *Vajra* and *Yava* Yogas as stated by ancient teachers (using phrases like "benefics in the ascendant and seventh"), interpreted them arbitrarily without considering the alternatives. He stated that if Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are in the 1st and 7th houses, and Saturn, Sun, and Mars are in the 4th and 10th houses, *Vajra Yoga* is formed. Subsequently, a doubt arose in his mind: "How can this combination occur?" This is because it places Mercury and Venus in the fourth house from the Sun, which is entirely impossible according to *Siddhanta* <note>mathematical astronomy</note>. The maximum distance of Mercury and Venus from the Sun is always less than two signs <note>approx. 48 degrees for Venus and 28 for Mercury</note>. Due to this doubt, he mentioned the subject here and shifted the blame for the error onto the ancient teachers. In Varahamihira's time, there was no astrologer greater than him, so everyone accepted his word. Even later, commentators like Bhattotpala did not pay attention to this discrepancy and simply supported Varahamihira's interpretation. || 6 ||

->Now, in the following Anustubh verse, he describes the four Yogas named Yupa, Ishu, Shakti, and Danda:<-

### If all planets are situated in four houses starting from the angles,
### They are called Yupa, Ishu, Shakti, and Danda respectively, beginning from the Ascendant. || 7 ||

**Commentary:** "Starting from the angles..." Starting from the *Hora* (Ascendant) and the other centers <term>Kendras: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</term> in sequence, if all planets are positioned across four houses, then the four Yogas named Yupa, Ishu, Shakti, and Danda occur. Specifically: When all planets are in the four houses starting from the 1st to the 4th (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th), it is **Yupa Yoga**. When all planets are in the four houses from the 4th to the 7th (4th, 5th, 6th, 7th), it is **Ishu** (or Shara) **Yoga**. When all planets are in the four houses from the 7th to the 10th (7th, 8th, 9th, 10th), it is **Shakti Yoga**. When all planets are in the four houses from the 10th to the 1st (10th, 11th, 12th, 1st), it is **Danda Yoga**. || 7 ||

**Vernacular Translation—** If all planets are located in the four places starting from the Ascendant to the fourth, it is *Yupa Yoga*; if all planets are in the four signs from the fourth to the seventh, it is *Shara Yoga*; if all planets are in the four houses from the seventh to the tenth, it is *Shakti Yoga*; and if all planets are in the four houses from the tenth to the Ascendant, it is called *Danda Yoga*. || 7 ||

# Chapter on Nabhasa Yogas in the Brihat Jataka

### Now, he describes the five yogas named Boat, Peak, Umbrella, Bow, and Half-Moon in the Anustubh meter—

->The Boat, Peak, Umbrella, and Bow are formed by the seven planets situated in seven houses in that same manner.<-
->The Half-Moon yoga is said to be formed by those same configurations starting from other houses. || 8 ||<-

**The Boat, Peak, and Umbrella:** In that same manner previously described, starting from the <term>Lagna</term><note>The Ascendant or 1st house</note> or the <term>Kendras</term><note>The angular houses: 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th</note>, when all seven planets are situated in seven continuous houses, the four yogas named Boat, Peak, Umbrella, and Bow are formed. 

Specifically: When all planets are in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th houses, it is called the **Boat** (<term>Nau</term>) yoga. Similarly, when all planets are in the 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, and 10th houses, it is the **Peak** (<term>Kuta</term>) yoga. Then, if all planets are in the 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th, and 1st houses, it is the **Umbrella** (<term>Chatra</term>) yoga. Finally, when all planets are in the 10th, 11th, 12th, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th houses, it is the **Bow** (<term>Chapa</term>) yoga.

**The Half-Moon:** The **Half-Moon** (<term>Ardha-chandra</term>) yoga is formed by these same configurations but starting from other houses. The Boat and others were said to start from the <term>Kantakas</term><note>Another term for the Kendras or angles</note>; when they start from other signs—namely starting from the <term>Panapharas</term><note>Succedent houses: 2nd, 5th, 8th, and 11th</note> or the <term>Apoklimas</term><note>Cadent houses: 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th</note>—and occupy seven continuous houses, it is called Half-Moon. This is of eight types:
1. From the 2nd to the 8th house.
2. From the 3rd to the 9th house.
3. From the 5th to the 11th house.
4. From the 6th to the 12th house.
5. From the 8th to the 2nd house.
6. From the 9th to the 3rd house.
7. From the 11th to the 5th house.
8. From the 12th to the 6th house. || 8 ||

**Vernacular Translation:** Following the previously mentioned method, if the seven planets occupy the seven houses starting from the Ascendant to the 7th, it is Boat yoga; from the 4th to the 10th, it is Peak yoga; from the 7th to the 1st, it is Umbrella yoga; and from the 10th to the 4th, it is Bow yoga. Furthermore, if the planets occupy seven continuous houses starting from a house other than a Kendra (i.e., a Panaphara or Apoklima), it is called the Half-Moon yoga. || 8 ||

### Now, he describes the two yogas named Ocean and Wheel in the Anustubh meter—

->The Ocean yoga is formed by planets in six alternating houses starting from the 2nd.<-
->The Wheel yoga is formed similarly starting from the Ascendant; this concludes the summary of the "Shape" yogas. || 9 ||<-

**Alternating:** Starting from the 2nd house, when the seven planets are situated in six alternating houses <note>e.g., 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th, 10th, and 12th</note>, the yoga is called **Ocean** (<term>Samudra</term>).

For example: When the seven planets are situated in the six houses—the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth—it is called **Samudra Yoga** <note>The "Ocean" combination</note>. Regarding the phrase "situated starting from the ascendant": in this same manner, when the seven planets are situated in six houses starting from the ascendant <term>Lagna|The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at birth</term> in every other house, it is called **Chakra Yoga** <note>The "Wheel" combination</note>. For example: when all the planets are in the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth, and eleventh houses, it is Chakra Yoga. In this way, the summary of the **Akriti Yogas** <note>Combinations based on the geometric shape or pattern formed by planets in the birth chart</note> has been explained. ||6||

**Vernacular Translation—** If all planets are in the six even houses (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) starting from the second house, it is **Samudra Yoga**. Similarly, if all planets are in the six odd houses (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) starting from the ascendant, it is **Chakra Yoga**. Thus, the collection of Shape Yogas is concluded here. ||6||

**Special Meaning—** A yoga named according to its shape (form) is called an **Akriti Yoga**. Here, twenty types of Shape Yogas, from Gada <note>Mace</note> to Chakra <note>Wheel</note>, have been described. ||6||

->Now, the seven Numerical Yogas are described in the Shalini meter:<-

### The Numerical Yogas occur when the seven planets occupy seven signs;
### By decreasing the count by one, they are: Vallaki, Damini,
### Pasha, Kedara, Shula, Yuga,
### and Gola—excluding those previously mentioned. ||10||

Regarding the **Sankhya Yogas** <note>Numerical combinations based simply on how many signs the planets occupy</note>: When the seven planets are placed in seven signs, and then by decreasing the number of signs one by one, seven Numerical Yogas occur. These range from Vallaki to Gola. Specifically: when all seven planets are in any seven houses, it is **Vallaki Yoga** <note>Lute combination</note>. When the seven planets are in six houses, it is **Damini Yoga** <note>Rope/Garland combination</note>. Similarly, in five houses, it is **Pasha Yoga** <note>Noose combination</note>. In four houses, it is **Kedara Yoga** <note>Field combination</note>. In three houses, it is **Shula Yoga** <note>Trident combination</note>. In two houses, it is **Yuga Yoga** <note>Yoke combination</note>. When all seven planets are in a single sign, it is **Gola Yoga** <note>Sphere/Globe combination</note>. These occur "excluding those previously mentioned"—meaning one should set aside the previously described yogas. This implies that if a planetary arrangement matches a previously defined specific yoga (like a Shape Yoga), that specific yoga takes precedence, and the Numerical Yoga name is not used. ||10||

**Vernacular Translation—** If the seven planets are in seven places, it is **Vallaki** (Vina) Yoga; if the seven planets are in 6 places, it is **Dama** Yoga; if all planets are in five places...

# Chapter on Nabhasa Yogas in the Brihat Jataka

If all planets are situated in 5 signs, it is called <term>Pasha Yoga</term> <note>The Noose</note>; if in 4 signs, it is <term>Kedara Yoga</term> <note>The Field</note>; if in 3 signs, it is <term>Shula</term> <note>The Trident</note>; if in 2 signs, it is <term>Yuga</term> <note>The Yoke</note>; and if all planets are in a single sign, it is called <term>Gola</term> <note>The Sphere</note> Yoga. In this manner, seven types of <term>Sankhya Yogas</term> <note>Numerical combinations based on the number of signs occupied</note> have been described. However, in these numerical combinations, if the characteristics of the previously mentioned Yupa, Isha, etc., or Naukuta, etc., are present, then one should not consider it a Sankhya Yoga, but rather the <term>Akriti Yoga</term> <note>Form-based combinations</note> such as Naukuta, etc., as defined by those previous characteristics. ||10||

**Special Meaning** — If planets are in all seven houses from the Ascendant to the seventh house, the Sankhya Yoga called <term>Vallaki</term> <note>The Lute</note> occurs. However, the characteristics of the <term>Nauka</term> <note>Boat</note> Akriti Yoga are also met in this position; therefore, in such a situation, one should understand it as Nauka Yoga, not Vallaki. This principle should be applied in other cases as well. ||10||

The author now describes the results for those born under the three Ashraya Yogas and the two Dala Yogas in the Vasantatilaka meter:

->**One born in Rajju is envious, fond of foreign lands, and loves wandering.**<-
->**In Mushala, one is proud, wealthy, and engaged in many activities.**<-
->**Born in Nala, one is deformed, steady, rich, and clever; in Srag,**<-
->**one enjoys pleasures; in Bhujaga, one suffers much misery. ||11||**<-

"Envious" etc. — One who is envious is jealous of the prosperity of others. "Fond of foreign lands" means having a nature to reside in foreign countries. "Loves wandering" means constantly traveling. Now, one might ask: if one resides in a foreign land, they are already a traveler; why mention both? It is said: even in a foreign land, one may reside in many different regions without being a constant traveler <note>The text distinguishes between living abroad and the act of constant movement</note>. Such is the person born in the Yoga called Rajju <note>The Rope</note>.

"Proud" means haughty; "Wealthy" means possessing riches; "Engaged in many activities" means one who starts many works or projects. Such is the person born in the Yoga called Mushala <note>The Pestle</note>.

"Deformed" means lacking a limb; "Steady" means firm in resolve; "Rich" means wealthy; "Clever" means having a subtle vision in tasks. Such is the person born in the Yoga called Nala <note>The Reed</note>. Thus, the results for those born in the three Ashraya Yogas are explained.

"In Srag, one enjoys pleasures" etc. — One born in Srag Yoga <note>The Garland</note> is endowed with enjoyments. One born in the Serpent Yoga called Bhujaga suffers much misery, experiencing various kinds of sorrows. Some read this in the plural: "Those born in Nala are deformed, steady, wealthy, and clever; those in Srag are endowed with pleasures; those in Bhujaga suffer much misery." There is no fault in this reading. Thus, the results for those born in the two Dala Yogas are explained. ||11||

**Vernacular Translation** — One born in <term>Rajju Yoga</term> is envious, lives in foreign lands, and is of a wandering nature. One born in <term>Mushala Yoga</term> is proud, wealthy, and [engaged in] many...

## With the Sanskrit Commentary of Bhattotpala and the Hindi Translation

...is the one who initiates actions. In the **Nala** <note>Reed</note> yoga, the person is physically impaired in some limb, yet possesses firm determination and is skilled in all works. In the **Mala** <note>Garland</note> yoga, one is a seeker of pleasures, and in the **Sarpa** <note>Serpent</note> yoga, the person born is a partaker of sorrows. ||11||

->Now, when other yogas and the **Ashraya** <note>Refuge/Support</note> yogas are seen at the same time,<-
->to resolve the contradiction of the Ashraya yoga, he speaks in the Anustubh meter:<-

->The results spoken for **Ashraya** yogas become fruitless when mixed with others;<-
->those with which they are mixed shall give the fruit, while unmixed, they grant their own results. ||12||

**The results spoken for Ashraya...** Where another yoga and an Ashraya yoga both occur, the Ashraya yoga becomes mixed with the other (such as the **Yava** <note>Barley</note> yoga, etc.). Due to this mixing, it becomes fruitless and does not grant its own specific result. In this way, when mixed with others, they become ineffective. Those yogas with which they have attained a similarity shall provide the fruit there. Some read "the fruit is theirs" for those with whom they are mixed. When they are "unmixed" by others, then they are "givers of their own fruit," meaning they grant their personal results. For instance, if the Ascendant is in a **Chara** <note>Moveable/Cardinal</note> sign, and planets are in Fixed or Dual signs, they are mixed. If the Ascendant is Fixed and planets are in Moveable or Dual signs, they are unmixed. If the Ascendant is Dual and planets are in Moveable or Fixed signs, they are unmixed. ||12||

**Vernacular:** In the **Ashraya** (namely **Rajju**, **Musala**, and **Nala**) yogas, if the characteristics of other yogas (such as **Akriti** <note>Shape</note> yogas) are also found, then the result of the Ashraya yoga does not occur; the result will be of that other yoga whose characteristics are present. Only if it is not joined by other characteristics does the Ashraya yoga give its own result. ||12||

*Special Meaning:* For example, if all planets are in the four Moveable signs and the Ascendant is also a Moveable sign, the characteristics of **Rajju** <note>Rope</note> are present, but the characteristics of **Kamala** <note>Lotus</note> yoga are also present. Therefore, in this case, only the result of the Lotus will manifest, not the Rope. If all planets are in Moveable signs but the Ascendant is a Fixed or Dual sign, in that situation, the result of the Rope yoga will occur. ||12||

->Now, he speaks in the Vasantatilaka meter regarding the nature of those<-
->born in the yogas named **Gada**, **Shakata**, **Vihaga**, **Shringataka**, and **Hala**:<-

->A performer of sacrifices, possessing wealth, and always interested in money in **Gada**;<-
->living by that means <note>carts</note>, sickly, and with a bad wife is one born in **Shakata**;<-
->a messenger, a wanderer, and a quarrel-maker is declared in **Vihaga**;<-
->one who is happy for a long time in **Shringataka**, and a farmer in the one called **Hala**. ||13||

**A performer of sacrifices...** *Yajva* means one inclined to perform sacrifices; *Arthabhak* means a vessel of wealth; *Satatam* means at all times; *Artharuchi* means one whose nature is to strive for the acquisition of wealth. Such a person is born in the yoga called **Gada** <note>Mace</note>. **Living by that means...** "That" refers to the **Shakata** <note>Wagon</note>. He enjoys the livelihood of the wagon; meaning, he becomes one who earns a living through carts. *Saruja* means afflicted by disease...

# The Chapter on Nabhasa Yogas in the Brihat Jataka

A person born under the **Shakata Yoga** <note>The "Wagon" configuration</note> has a "bad wife" <note>original: "kudāraḥ kutsitabhāryaḥ"</note> and possesses such qualities. He is a messenger and a wanderer. A messenger is one who travels to others to deliver messages; a wanderer is one who is constantly roaming. Now, one might argue that a messenger must necessarily be a wanderer. To this, it is said: a messenger travels by the will of others, whereas this person wanders by his own will—he possesses both traits. He is a "quarrel-maker" <note>original: "kalahakṛt"</note>, meaning he is prone to disputes; such is the person born in the **Vihaga Yoga** <note>The "Bird" configuration</note>. It is "declared" or stated as such. "Happy after a long time" <note>original: "cireṇa sukhī"</note> means he becomes happy at the end of his life; such is the person born in the **Shringataka Yoga** <note>The "Horned/Triangle" configuration</note>. Others have interpreted this yoga as simply "long-term happiness," but that is incorrect. For the Lord Garga says: "When planets are situated in the Ascendant, the fifth, and the ninth houses, it is known as Shringataka Yoga. Those born under it are happy at the end of their lives and are sweet-spoken." One born in the **Hala Yoga** <note>The "Plow" configuration</note> is a "tiller of the earth," meaning he practices agriculture. || 13 ||

**Vernacular Translation:** A man born in **Gada Yoga** <note>The "Mace" configuration</note> performs sacrifices, is wealthy, and is always intent on earning money. One born in **Shakata Yoga** earns a living through carts/wagons, is sickly, and has a wicked wife. In **Vihaga Yoga**, one is a messenger, a wanderer, and a quarrelsome person. In **Shringataka Yoga**, one is happy at the end of life. And a man born in **Hala Yoga** is a farmer. || 13 ||

->Now, he describes the nature of those born in the Vajra, Yava, Padma, and Vapi Yogas using the Vasantatilaka meter:<-

> In **Vajra**, one is happy at the beginning and end of life, <gloss>1</gloss> lovely, and very brave.
> In **Yava**, one is powerful and happy in the middle of life.
> In **Padma**, one has world-renowned fame and boundless happiness and virtues.
> In **Vapi**, one has small but steady happiness; he accumulates wealth but is not a giver. || 14 ||

Regarding "Happy at the end and beginning" in **Vajra Yoga** <note>The "Diamond/Thunderbolt" configuration</note>: This means one is happy in childhood, suffers in youth, and becomes happy again in old age. He is "lovely" <note>original: "subhagaḥ"</note>, meaning dear to all people, and "very brave," meaning exceptionally steady in battle. Such is the person born in the Vajra Yoga. He is "endowed with power" or valor. The word *atha* is used here to complete the meter. "At the end of age" <note>original: "vayo'ntaḥ"</note> here serves as a synonym for the "middle of life." Such is the person born in the **Yava Yoga** <note>The "Barley-corn" configuration</note>. "World-renowned fame" means his fame is celebrated by all people. One might ask: is such fame always present? It is said: it exists in certain cases. For instance, even with hundreds of fame-seeking actions, some do not achieve great renown, [but this person does]. "Boundless happiness and virtues" means his joy and qualities are immeasurable. Virtues include learning, bravery, and so on; such is the person born in the **Padma Yoga** <note>The "Lotus" configuration</note>. "Small and steady happiness" <note>original: "tanusthirasukham"</note> means the happiness is slight but lasts for a long time...

### Commentary in Sanskrit and Hindi by Bhattotpala

One who has happiness, meaning their happiness is slight but lasts for a long time. A "hoarder" <note>original: nidhikṛt</note> is one who is inclined to bury wealth in the ground; not a giver, but a miser. Such a person is born under the configuration known as **Vapi** (The Well) Yoga. — 14

**Vernacular Translation** — A person born in the **Vajra** (Diamond) Yoga is happy in the final stages of life; that is, they remain unhappy in youth, but are handsome, brave, and strong. A person born in the **Yava** (Barley) Yoga is happy in the middle of their life. One born in the **Kamala** (Lotus) Yoga is of renowned fame, possesses extreme happiness, and is endowed with many virtues. One born in the **Vapi** (Well) Yoga possesses small but steady happiness, is one who buries and hides wealth, and does not give even a single penny to anyone. — 14

Now, the nature of those born in the four configurations of **Yupa**, **Shara**, **Shakti**, and **Danda** is described in the *Vasantatilaka* meter:

->**The one in Yupa is generous, self-controlled, and performs the best sacrifices;**<-
->**In Shara, one is cruel, a prison warden, or a maker of arrows.**<-
->**In Shakti, one is lowly, lazy, and devoid of happiness and wealth;**<-

Regarding "Generous and self-controlled": One who is a giver, self-possessed <note>original: ātmavān, meaning vigilant or prudent</note>, and performs the best of sacrifices <note>term: Krutu-vara; refers to Vedic sacrificial rituals</note> is born in the **Yupa** (Sacrificial Post) Yoga. Regarding "Cruel": One who is violent or delights in killing, a "guardian of secrets" <note>original: guptyadhikṛtaḥ, interpreted here as a jailer or warden</note>, or an arrow-maker is born in the **Shara** (Arrow) Yoga. Regarding "Lowly": One who performs base deeds or associates with the low-minded, is lazy or unskilled in actions, and is "devoid of happiness and wealth"—meaning lacking in enjoyment and finances—is born in the **Shakti** (Spear) Yoga. One who is "separated from loved ones" such as sons and family, and follows a "menial life"—meaning the life of a servant or a laborer <note>original: śūdravṛtti</note>—is the man born in the **Danda** (Staff) Yoga. — 15

One born in the **Shara** Yoga is violent, the owner of a prison, and a maker of arrows. The person born in the **Shakti** Yoga is lowly, lazy, and destitute of happiness and wealth. One born in the **Danda** Yoga is deprived of his dear ones and works in service/employment. — 15

# Chapter on Nabhasa Yogas in the Brihat Jataka

**One born with the Fame and Unstable Happiness...** One endowed with fame is of renowned reputation. "Unstable happiness" means sometimes happy and sometimes miserable. He is also "miserly," meaning ungenerous; the word "and" here serves as a conjunction. Such is the person born in the **Nauka (Boat) Yoga**. <note>Nauka Yoga occurs when all planets occupy the first seven houses starting from the Ascendant.</note>

**In the Kuta Yoga, one is untruthful...** One whose mind is inclined toward falsehood is a speaker of lies. He is also a "jailer" <note>original: bandhanapa</note>. Some read the text as "one born in Kuta is a lying, miserly jailer." Such is the person born in the **Kuta (Peak) Yoga**. This concludes the Kuta Yoga.

**Born in the Chatra Yoga...** One who brings happiness to his own kin is a "benefactor of kinsmen." He possesses "end-of-life happiness," meaning he is happy in his old age. Such is the person born in the **Chatra (Umbrella) Yoga**. This concludes the Chatra Yoga.

**Born in the Karmuka Yoga...** He is brave and a lover of battle. He possesses "beginning and end happiness," meaning he is happy in his early childhood and happy in his old age. Such is the person born in the **Karmuka (Bow) Yoga**, also known as the Chapa Yoga. This concludes the Chapa Yoga. || 16 ||

**Vernacular Translation—** One born in the **Nauka Yoga** is endowed with fame, has unstable happiness (meaning sometimes joy, sometimes sorrow), and is miserly. One born in the **Kuta Yoga** is a liar and the master of a prison. In the **Chatra Yoga**, the native brings happiness to his family and finds happiness in the final stage of life. In the **Chapa (Bow) Yoga**, the native is brave and happy in childhood and old age—implying he is unhappy in middle age. || 16 ||

Now, the author describes the nature of those born in the **Ardha-chandra**, **Samudra**, **Chakra**, and **Vallaki** Yogas using the *Vasantatilaka* meter:

-> One born in the **Half-Moon** is lovely, of beautiful body, and eminent; <-
-> In the **Abode of Waters**, one is like a king and an enjoyer; <-
-> In the **Wheel**, one has feet colored by the luster of the crowns of kings; <-
-> And one born in the **Lute** is skillful and fond of song and dance. || 17 ||

**Born in the Half-Moon...** "Lovely" means dear to all people. "Beautiful body" means handsome to look upon. "Eminent" means respected by everyone. Such is the person born in the **Ardha-chandra (Half-Moon) Yoga**.

**Like a king...** Equal to a ruler and an "enjoyer" (one who possesses luxuries). Such is the person born in the **Abode of Waters** <note>original: toyālaya</note>, also known as the **Samudra (Ocean) Yoga**.

**In the Wheel...** "Kings" are rulers; their "crowns" are their headpieces; the "luster" is the brilliance of the crest-jewels. One whose "feet are colored" or smeared by that brilliance—this means that kings fall at his feet, signifying he becomes a supreme emperor <note>original: mahārājādhirāja</note>. Alternatively, it may mean he is worthy of worship by kings due to his penance or knowledge. Such is the person born in the **Chakra (Wheel) Yoga**.

The results for the twenty **Akriti Yogas** <term>Akriti Yoga: "Shape" configurations where planets form specific geometric patterns in the birth chart</term> have now been explained. Following this, the results for the yogas indicating the number of kings will be explained.

**Born in the Lute...** Skillful...

...possessing subtle vision, a lover of songs and dance; one born in the **Veena Yoga** <note>The "Lute" configuration, where planets are distributed in seven signs</note> becomes such a person. || 17 ||

**Vernacular Translation —** A person born in the **Ardhachandra Yoga** <note>Half-Moon configuration</note> is beloved by all, beautiful, radiant, and a leader (highly respected). A person born in the **Samudra Yoga** <note>Ocean configuration</note>, even if from a poor family, becomes like a king and an enjoyer of life's pleasures. A person born in the **Chakra Yoga** <note>Wheel configuration</note> is worthy of worship by kings (either a universal emperor or a teacher to kings due to specialized knowledge). A person born in the **Veena Yoga** possesses a subtle intellect and delights in the arts of singing and dance. || 17 ||

Now, the author describes the nature of those born in the **Damini**, **Pasha**, **Kedara**, and **Shula** Yogas using the *Vasantatilaka* meter:

->**In the Damni Yoga, one is a donor, devoted to the work of others, and a protector of cattle.**<-
->**In Pasha, one is unscrupulous in earning wealth, though surrounded by servants and kin.**<-
->**Born in Kedara, one is an agriculturalist and very useful to many. In Shula, one is brave,**<-
->**scarred, desirous of wealth, yet remains destitute.**<- || 18 ||

**Commentary:** "A donor" means generous; "devoted to the work of others" means intent on philanthropy; "protector of cattle" means a guardian of animals or one possessing many cattle. Alternatively, in some readings, it means a protector or sustainer of many people—essentially a village headman. Such is the one born in the **Damni** <note>also called Damini or "Rope"</note> Yoga. Regarding **Pasha** <note>"Noose"</note>: "Unscrupulous in earning wealth" means one who acquires money through improper or immoral means; his servants and kinsmen are of the same nature. Such is the one born in the Pasha Yoga. Regarding **Kedara** <note>"Field"</note>: "An agriculturalist" is one who farms; "useful to many" means he performs good deeds that benefit a great number of people. Such is the one born in the Kedara Yoga. In **Shula** <note>"Spear"</note>: "Brave" means courageous in battle; "scarred" means wounded by weapons; "desirous of wealth" means fond of money (some read this as "fond of violence"). "Destitute" means poor. Such is the one born in the Shula Yoga. || 18 ||

**Vernacular Translation —** One born in the **Dam Yoga** is a donor, a philanthropist, and a rearer of livestock. One born in the **Pasha Yoga**, along with his circle of servants and relatives, is devoid of character in the accumulation of wealth; that is, he abandons shame and gains wealth through injustice. One born in the **Kedara Yoga** is a farmer and a benefactor to many. A person born in the **Shula Yoga** is fond of war, has a body scarred by weapons, desires wealth, yet is always penniless. || 18 ||

<header>The Chapter on Celestial Combinations in the Brihat Jataka</header>

->Now, in the Harini meter, the author describes the nature of the Yuga and Gola combinations, and explains how all Celestial combinations yield results throughout all planetary periods (Dashas):<-

### One born under the Yuga combination is destitute or a heretic; while under the Gola combination,
### one is penniless, filthy, ignorant, a poor craftsman, lazy, and a wanderer.
### Thus have the Celestial combinations been described here along with their fruits;
### these must be considered as giving certain results throughout all planetary periods. ||19||

->*Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Celestial Combinations," in the Brihat Jataka composed by the illustrious teacher Varahamihira.*<-

**Destitute of wealth** etc. — One born in the combination called **Yuga** <note>Yuga-yoga: A configuration where all planets are placed in only two signs.</note> becomes destitute of wealth (penniless) and a **heretic** <note>original: "pakhandi"</note>, meaning one who has strayed from the path of the three Vedas. The word "or" in the verse here functions as "and"—implying he is both penniless and a heretic. The word "then" denotes the next sequence. One born in the combination called **Gola** <note>Gola-yoga: A configuration where all planets are restricted to a single sign.</note> is **penniless**, **filthy** (having a dirty body or wearing soiled clothes), **ignorant** (a fool), a **poor craftsman** (performing crafts that are despised in the world), **lazy** (incapable of action), and a **wanderer**. 

Now, one might ask: are "lazy" and "wanderer" not contradictory? It is explained thus: by nature he is lazy, yet due to extreme poverty, he is unable to obtain food without moving about; therefore, he is a wanderer. In this way, the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of the seven "Numerical Combinations" <note>Sankhya-yogas</note> have been explained.

**Thus have the combinations been described** etc. — In this manner, the Celestial combinations <note>term: Nabhasa-yogas (Special planetary configurations that depend on the shape or number of signs occupied, rather than specific house placements)</note> have been stated along with their fruits. In this chapter, these are to be understood as **giving certain results throughout all planetary periods** <note>term: Dashas (Specific blocks of time in a person's life ruled by a particular planet)</note>, meaning they provide results at all times. 

One might object: for combinations like the "Thunderbolt" <note>Vajra-yoga</note>, it was stated that the person is happy at the beginning and end of life; how then can it be said they act "throughout all periods"? It is replied: according to those specific statements, happiness or sorrow will occur at the times indicated. For those combinations where no specific time division was mentioned, they will provide happiness or sorrow as described throughout all the planetary periods of their life. 

One might further object: does anyone's entire life pass in a single uniform state of happiness or sorrow? Even the wealthy are overcome by mental grief, and even those who live on alms may sometimes feel satisfied, such as when resting in the cool shade of a tree. Since happiness and sorrow are experienced in alternating turns by all worldly beings, how can these combinations be "constant" throughout all periods? 

It is replied: these combinations do not destroy or cancel out the results of the planetary periods <note>Dashas</note> or the "Eightfold Points" <note>term: Ashtakavarga (A system of points used to calculate the strength of planets and houses)</note>. The lord of a planetary period gives results—whether good or bad—based on the Eightfold Points. Therefore, while the specific timing of events is governed by those systems, the general influence of these Celestial combinations persists throughout the entire life. Thus, a mixture of experiences is possible for both the wealthy and the poor. 

Thus has the Chapter on Celestial Combinations been explained. Regarding what was promised to be discussed earlier in this chapter: it is noted that the "Half-Moon" <note>Dala</note> and "Angular" <note>Akriti</note> combinations cannot occur simultaneously...

# Page 275

The simultaneous occurrence of <term>Ashraya Yogas</term><note>Planetary combinations based on the nature of the signs (movable, fixed, or dual) they occupy.</note> does not happen. If <term>Dala Yogas</term><note>Combinations involving only benefics or only malefic planets in specific houses.</note> occur alongside <term>Sankhya Yogas</term><note>Combinations based simply on the number of signs occupied by the seven planets.</note>, then only the result of the Dala Yoga manifests. Similarly, if <term>Akriti Yogas</term><note>Combinations where planets form specific geometric shapes in the birth chart.</note> are joined with Sankhya Yogas, the result of the Akriti Yoga prevails because it acts as an exception to the Sankhya Yogas. 

Aside from those previously mentioned, there is also an exception for the Ashraya Yogas. Indeed, Ashraya Yogas become fruitless when mixed with others. Therefore, Sankhya Yogas and Ashraya Yogas are superseded. If a Sankhya Yoga occurs alongside an Ashraya Yoga, the Ashraya Yoga alone prevails. 

Now, one might ask: if both Ashraya and Sankhya Yogas are subject to similar rules of exception, how is it that the Sankhya Yoga is superseded by the Ashraya Yoga? It is said: if a Sankhya Yoga exists where an Ashraya Yoga is present, the Sankhya Yoga is recognized. However, if it occurs through an Ashraya Yoga, then the scope for the Ashraya Yoga is naturally established. When an Ashraya Yoga takes the place of a Sankhya Yoga, there remains another scope for the Sankhya Yoga. But when all planets are in a single sign, the Sankhya Yoga is superseded by the Ashraya Yoga; in that case, there would be no scope for the <term>Golaka</term><note>A specific Sankhya Yoga where all planets are in one sign.</note> position at all. This follows the interpretive rule: "Rules that have no other scope of application supersede those that do."

Now, according to the <term>Purana Yavana</term><note>The "Ancient Greeks" or early Greco-Indian astrological authorities.</note> school of thought, the one hundred and fifty Yogas related to each individual sign and the Ascendant are demonstrated. Among them, there are twenty-three Akriti Yogas; Varahamihira, however, has mentioned only twenty. But from among those, four Yogas are described starting with the <term>Gada Yoga</term>. When all planets are in the Ascendant and the fourth house, it is Gada Yoga. In the fourth and seventh, it is <term>Shankha</term>. In the seventh and tenth, it is <term>Babhruka</term>. In the tenth and the Ascendant, it is <term>Dhvaja</term>. Thus, the twenty previously mentioned, together with Shankha, Babhruka, and Dhvaja, make twenty-three. 

The Sankhya Yogas number one hundred and twenty-seven; when added to others to reach one hundred and fifty, and multiplied by the twelve signs, they become eighteen hundred (1800). The derivation of these one hundred and twenty-seven Sankhya Yogas is shown here. Their mathematical combinations are as follows:
- Combinations of one: 7
- Combinations of two: 21
- Combinations of three: 35
- Combinations of four: 35
- Combinations of five: 21
- Combinations of six: 7
- Combinations of seven: 1
Totaling these together, they become one hundred and twenty-seven (127). 

Varahamihira stated this very point in his *Vivaha-patala*: "Why were the one hundred and twenty-seven combinations of two, three, etc., planets in the Ascendant not mentioned?" Now, the mathematics of combinations (<term>Vikalpa-ganita</term>) is demonstrated. The Teacher has explained this calculation in the *Samhita*: "By adding the previous term to the one following, excluding the last place, they declare the number. By leading the desired combinations in sequence..."

It also introduces the mathematical derivation of 127 planetary combinations based on the "Ancient Yavana" system.</summary>

# Chapter on Nabhasa Yogas in the Brihat Jataka
<page-num>276</page-num>

-> "When one is removed, there is a cessation; then another method follows." <-

<note>This quote refers to the iterative process of combinatorial mathematics used in ancient Indian astrology.</note>

Here, to determine the number of possible combinations <term>vikalpa: mathematical permutations or combinations</term>, one should place the numbers starting from one upwards, up to the total number desired. For example, with the seven planets, we set down the numbers from one to seven: 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. In this method, a position is added to the previous result, excluding the final one. "Previous result" refers to the sum obtained in the preceding step; by adding this to the next position while excluding the last, the calculation proceeds. 

First, take the number one at the bottom and add it to the two positions above it. Thus, three units are produced; these should be added to the three positions above them. Thus, six are produced; these should be added to the four positions above them. Thus, ten units are produced; these should be added to the five positions above them. There, fifteen are produced; these should be added to the six positions above them. There, twenty-one are produced. Beyond this, as the operation ends, only seven remain above. As stated, "excluding the final position," by repeating this process from the bottom up, thirty-five are produced in the fifth place, thirty-five again in the fourth, twenty-one in the third, seven in the second, and only one in the first: 7, 21, 35, 35, 21, 7, 1. <note>This describes the construction of what is known in modern mathematics as Pascal's Triangle to find binomial coefficients.</note>

Alternatively, there is another method for calculating the numbers:

> "Having placed them in reverse order, place the natural order below. Multiply by the natural order and divide by the number situated below."

The layout is as follows: Here, the number one is the divisor for the seven. By dividing, we get seven (7). Multiplying this by the six in the second position and dividing by the two situated below, the result is twenty-one (21). Multiplying this by the five in the third position and dividing by three, the result is thirty-five (35). Multiplying this by the four in the fourth position and dividing by four, the result is thirty-five (35). Multiplying by the next and dividing by five, the result is twenty-one (21). Multiplying this by two and dividing by six, the result is seven. Multiplying this by one and dividing by seven, the result is exactly one. These are the combinations for groups of one, two, three, four, five, six, and seven planets. Having performed this combinatorial mathematics, one should explain the desired numbers. Now, the extraction of these combinations should be done using the "clod-of-earth" distribution method <term>loṣṭa-prastāra: a visualization technique using pebbles or markers to map out combinations</term>.

> "By leading the desired combinations in order, when one is removed, there is a cessation; then another method follows."

One should write the initial letters of the desired combinations. Among the single combinations, create the variations by placing a single marker. In the double combinations, keep the first marker fixed and produce variations with the second marker. Similarly, in combinations of three or more, keep the first marker fixed and produce other variations with the remaining moving markers. Having done this, the first one should be set aside. Because of the statement "when one is removed, there is a cessation," one should place the third by making a different mark. Because of the statement "then another method follows." It has also been said by the venerable Bhatta Shri Shankara:

> "The number of cells is called the number of syllables... <unclear>the rest of the verse is truncated</unclear>"

<summary>This page explains the mathematical procedures for calculating planetary combinations (Yogas) using two methods: an additive method similar to Pascal's Triangle and a multiplicative/divisive method for binomial coefficients. It also introduces the "loṣṭa-prastāra" or pebble-graph method for visualizing these permutations.</summary>

**Vernacular Translation—** In the <term>Yuga Yoga</term> <note>a specific planetary alignment where planets occupy only two signs</note>, one is destitute and a critic of the Vedas and sacred scriptures. And one born in the <term>Gola Yoga</term> <note>where all planets occupy a single sign</note> is poor, has an unclean body, is ignorant, performs blameworthy deeds, is lazy (incapable of work), and wanders aimlessly. The thirty-two <term>Nabhasa Yogas</term> <note>Celestial/Sky formations</note> mentioned in this chapter along with their results are certainly fruitful throughout all <term>dashas</term> <note>planetary periods; here meaning throughout the entire lifespan</note>. 16.

**Special Meaning—** It is stated here that these Nabhasa Yogas are fruitful in all planetary periods. However, the result for <term>Vajra Yoga</term> is said to be "happy in the early and late stages of life," and for <term>Yava Yoga</term>, "happy only in middle age." How then can they be consistently fruitful in all periods? The solution is this: the result occurs during the specific time mentioned for that particular Yoga. For those Yogas where no specific time is mentioned, the result is constant. Because these Yogas are formed by the connection of all planets, it is possible for their effects to manifest during the periods of all planets. For example, if a person is born in <term>Maala Yoga</term>, they are described as an "enjoyer"; such a person will find ways to enjoy life even if they are poor. Similarly, one born in <term>Sarpa Yoga</term> will remain a sufferer of distress even if they are wealthy. One should understand the matter by considering these points. 16.

# Chapter 13: On Lunar Combinations (Chandra-Yoga)

Now, the chapter on Lunar Combinations is explained. At the very beginning, the author of the *Malini* meter describes the nature of a person born when the Moon is situated in a Center (Kendras), a Succeedent (Panapharas), or a Cadent (Apoklimas) house relative to the Sun:

->**Modest, middling, and excellent are**<-
->**one’s humility, wealth, knowledge, and skill,**<-
->**when the Moon is in a Center and so on from the Sun.**<-
->**If by day or night the Moon is in its own or a great friend’s division,**<-
->**beheld by Jupiter or Venus, one becomes wealthy and happy. || 1 ||**<-

**Modest, middling, and excellent:** Humility <note>original: *vinaya*</note> refers to ethics and good character; wealth <note>original: *vitta*</note> refers to riches; knowledge <note>original: *jnana*</note> refers to scientific understanding and comprehension of the scriptures; intelligence <note>original: *dhi*</note> and skill <note>original: *naipunya*</note> refer to the ability to see the subtle details in tasks. When the Moon <note>original: *shashini*</note> is placed in a Center, Succeedent, or Cadent house relative to the Sun <note>original: *arkat*</note>, the humility, wealth, knowledge, and skill of the person born are respectively modest, middling, and excellent <note>low, medium, and high</note>.

This is what is meant: For one whose Moon is in a Center <note>1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th house</note> from the Sun at birth, these qualities like humility are "modest." This modesty implies a relative lack of them, as Yavanesvara <note>The "Lord of the Greeks," an early authority on Indian astrology</note> says:
> "The Moon situated in the four Centers from the Sun produces those who are foolish, poor, fickle, and lacking in character."

For one whose Moon is in a Succeedent house <note>2nd, 5th, 8th, or 11th</note> from the Sun at birth, these qualities are middling. This means they are not excessively present. For one whose Moon is in a Cadent house <note>3rd, 6th, 9th, or 12th</note> at birth, these qualities like humility are "excellent" (superior). Thus Yavanesvara says:
> "In the second [type of house], it produces wealthy men; in the Cadent houses, it produces those who are the best of their noble families."

**By day and so on:** When the Moon is in its own or a great friend’s Navamsha <note>a 1/9th divisional chart</note>, and is beheld by Jupiter or Venus during the day or night respectively, the person born becomes wealthy and happy (enjoying life's pleasures).

This is what is meant: If a person is born during the day and the Moon is in its own Navamsha or in the Navamsha of a great friend and is aspected (seen) by Jupiter <note>the Guru of the Gods</note>, then that person becomes wealthy and happy. If a person is born at night and the Moon is in its own or a great friend’s Navamsha and is aspected by Venus, then the person born becomes wealthy and happy. Some interpret the phrase "by day and night" as applying to the Moon's position in its own or a great friend's division regardless of the aspecting planet, but this is incorrect. For the Sage Garga says:
> "If the Moon is in its own division or a great friend's division during the day and is seen by Jupiter, the one born is endowed with wealth and happiness. If the Moon is so seen by Venus at night, it is praised at birth. If the Moon is in the opposite condition, men are born with little wealth."

And so says Yavanesvara:
> "The Moon in its own division, its form seen by Venus at night, is declared to bring forth a lordly person. But that same Moon brings about the highest prosperity if seen by the Priest of the Gods (Jupiter) during the day." || 1 ||

<summary>This page introduces the effects of the Moon's position relative to the Sun, explaining how its placement in different house types determines a person's character and wealth. It also details specific auspicious combinations involving Jupiter and Venus based on whether the birth occurs during the day or night.</summary>

# Chapter on Lunar Combinations in the Brihat Jataka

**Commentary—** If the Moon is in a <term>Kendra</term> (the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th house) from the Sun, then the person's character, wealth, knowledge of the scriptures, intelligence, and skill in work are all inferior or meager. If the Sun is in a <term>Panaphara</term> (the 2nd, 5th, 8th, or 11th house) relative to the Moon, the aforementioned qualities like humility and wealth are of a medium grade. If the Moon is in an <term>Apoklima</term> (the 3rd, 6th, 9th, or 12th house) from the Sun, then the person's character and wealth are excellent. Furthermore, if the Moon is in its own <term>Navamsha</term> <note>a one-ninth divisional chart sign</note> or in the Navamsha of a great friend, and is aspected by Jupiter during the day or by Venus at night, the person born is wealthy and happy. ||1||

->Now, the author describes the combination known as *Adhi Yoga* and its results in the *Vasantatilaka* meter:<-

**When the benefics occupy the 7th, 6th, and 8th houses from the Moon, it is called *Adhi Yoga*. Under this yoga, one is born as a commander of an army, a minister, or a king. Such individuals are endowed with happiness and prosperity, have their enemies destroyed, live long lives, and are free from the fear of disease. ||2||**

**Regarding the benefics:** This means that when the benefics—Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—are in the 7th, 6th, and 8th houses from the Moon, whether spread across all three houses, in two of them, or all in just one, the combination called *Adhi Yoga* is explained. Here, some interpret *Adhi Yoga* as occurring only when all three benefic planets are present without any gaps in the 6th, 7th, and 8th houses. However, this is incorrect. As *Shrutakirti* <note>an ancient authority on astrology</note> states:

> "When the 8th, 7th, and 6th houses from the Moon's position are joined by benefics, it is called *Adhi Yoga*; it was described by the ancients in seven ways in the extensive works."

In the "extensive works" (the *Vyasakriti*), the ancient teachers have described seven types. They are as follows: 1. When all benefics are in the 6th house; 2. When in the 7th; 3. When in the 8th; 4. When in the 6th and 7th; 5. When in the 6th and 8th; 6. When in the 7th and 8th; 7. When in the 6th, 7th, and 8th. In these positions, the benefics form *Adhi Yoga*. Furthermore, if malefic planets are in these positions, it is a "Malefic Adhi Yoga." If mixed, it is a "Mixed Adhi Yoga." As *Shrutakirti* also says:

> "Benefics in the 6th, 7th, and 8th from the Moon create a Benefic Adhi Yoga. Malefics create a Malefic one, and mixed planets create a Mixed one."

The author now describes the results for those born under *Adhi Yoga*: "born as a commander, minister, or king." One born under this *Adhi Yoga* becomes a commander of an army (*Chamupa*), a minister (*Sachiva*), or a protector of the earth (*Kshitipala*), meaning a king. Since these cannot all happen simultaneously, they are explained as distinct possibilities. Thus says *Badarayana* <note>another revered sage in the astrological tradition</note>:

> "When benefics are in the 6th, 7th, or 8th from the Moon, the person born should be known as a king or a minister."

<summary>This page explains how the Moon's position relative to the Sun determines the quality of a person's life and details the "Adhi Yoga," a powerful configuration where planets in the 6th, 7th, and 8th houses from the Moon grant high status and health.</summary>

...or even a commander of an army." This implies the following: if Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus possess superior strength, a king is born; if they have medium strength, a minister; and if they have low strength, a commander of an army. Those born under any of these variations of the combination become endowed with wealth and happiness, destroy their enemies, enjoy long lives, and remain free from disease and fear. In the opinion of some authorities, this is strictly a "Royal Combination" <note>original: "Rajayoga"</note>. Thus, it is stated in the *Saravali*: "If all the benefic planets occupy the 6th, 7th, and 8th houses from the Moon, and are not under the influence of malefic planets nor near the Sun, a king is born whose army's intoxicated elephants produce so much rutting-fluid that it is drunk by bees at the edges of the ocean forests."

Similarly, Mandavya states: "If all benefics occupy the 6th, 7th, or 8th houses from the Moon, they produce a ruler. The fire of his majesty burns so fiercely in the hearts of his enemies that their tears of sorrow act like offerings of clarified butter <note>original: "ghrita" or ghee</note> poured into a flame." ||2||

**Vernacular Translation—** If all benefic planets (Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus) are in the 6th, 7th, and 8th positions from the Moon, a commander, a minister, or a king is born. That is, if the benefics are weak, a commander; if of medium strength, a minister; and if fully strong, a king is born. Furthermore, one born in this combination <note>original: "Yoga"</note> is endowed with happiness and prosperity, is free from enemies, has a long life, and a healthy body. ||2||

**Special Meaning—** Here, some commentators opine that "Adhi Yoga" only occurs when all three planets occupy all three houses (6th, 7th, and 8th) simultaneously. However, such an interpretation contradicts the views of other teachers, such as Shrutakirti and others:

<margin>Benefic Adhi Yoga occurs when benefics are in the 6th, 7th, and 8th from the Moon. Malefic Adhi Yoga occurs with malefics in those spots, and a Mixed Yoga occurs with a mixture of both. ||2||</margin>

Now, the author describes the four combinations known as Sunapha, Anapha, Durudhara, and Kemadruma using the *Shardulavikridita* meter:

<margin>(1) The reading "The famous saying is not that" is more appropriate.</margin>

### Excluding the Sun, the Sunapha, Anapha, and Durudhara Yogas are formed by planets in the 2nd, 12th, or both positions
### from the Moon. Otherwise, many call it Kemadruma.
### If a planet is in a cardinal house from the Moon, or joined with it, Kemadruma is not recognized.
### Some say this applies to the cardinal houses of the Ninth-Division chart <note>original: "Navamsha"</note>, but that claim is not widely accepted (1). ||3||

**Excluding the Sun...** This means that excluding the Sun <note>original: "Arka"</note>, when any other planet like Mars etc., is in the 2nd, the 12th, or both positions from the Moon, the three Yogas called Sunapha, Anapha, and Durudhara are formed. This is what is meant: excluding the Sun, when any other planet is in the 2nd house from the Moon, then...

# Chapter on Lunar Combinations in the Brihat Jataka
<page-num>282</page-num>

The **Sunapha** <note>A yoga formed by planets in the 2nd house from the Moon</note> combination occurs when a planet is present in the second house from the Moon. When any planet, excluding the Sun, is in the twelfth house from the Moon, the **Anapha** <note>A yoga formed by planets in the 12th house from the Moon</note> combination occurs. Similarly, when planets (excluding the Sun) are present in both the second and twelfth houses from the Moon, the **Durudhara** <note>A yoga formed by planets in both the 2nd and 12th houses from the Moon</note> combination occurs. In these three combinations, if the Sun happens to be in the second or twelfth house, it does not cause the combination to break; however, the Sun is simply not counted among the planets that *create* the combination. This means: whether the Sun is in the second or twelfth house or not, if Mars and the other planets are situated there, they become the creators of the specified combination. These combinations have been taught by many teachers; otherwise, the **Kemadruma** <note>A combination signifying poverty or lack of support</note> is said to exist.

If not even one of these three combinations is present, then the combination called **Kemadruma** occurs. It is said: if there are planets in the "angles" <term>Kendra: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</term> of the Moon, or if the Moon is joined with another planet, the Kemadruma is not desired <note>meaning it is cancelled or neutralized</note>. This is the specific opinion of other sages such as **Garga**. According to them, if there are planets in the angles of the birth ascendant or if the Moon is joined with Mars or other planets, then even if the second and twelfth houses from the Moon are devoid of planets, Kemadruma does not occur. Regarding the phrase "joined with planets in the angles," some have interpreted this to mean only the angles from the Moon, but that is improper. If the Moon is joined with a planet, the combination is already included; therefore, saying "joined with the Moon" would be redundant. On this matter, the venerable **Garga** says:

> "If there is no planet other than the Sun in the twelfth, second, or the angles from the Moon; or if there is no planet in the angles from the ascendant excluding the Moon; then the combination named **Kemadruma** occurs, which is considered contemptible. Those born under it follow degraded conduct and are joined with the calamity of poverty."

Similarly, in the **Saravali** <note>A classic 8th-century astrological text by Kalyanavarman</note>:

> "**Sunapha**, **Anapha**, and **Durudhara** occur respectively when planets excluding the Sun are in the wealth (2nd), final (12th), or both houses from the Friend of the Night (the Moon). By this logic, when these combinations are absent and the Moon is devoid of planets in its angles, it is the very painful **Kemadruma**, especially if the Moon is not aspected by any planets."

Thus, "Kemadruma is not desired if there are planets in the angles or joined with the Moon." Other teachers do not wish for its presence under these conditions. However, **Varahamihira** <note>The 6th-century author of this text</note> indeed accepts its existence. This sentence is his own regarding that meaning. Otherwise, after stating "Kemadruma," he has merely cited the opinions of others. By others, it is said: "Kemadruma is not desired if there are planets in the angles or joined with the Moon." Even in his *Svalpa Jataka* <note>A shorter version of this work</note>, he stated that Kemadruma exists in the absence of Sunapha, Anapha, and Durudhara. As it is said:

> "**Anapha** is from planets in the twelfth excluding the Sun; **Sunapha** from those in the second from the Moon; **Durudhara** when they are in both. Any other state is known as **Kemadruma**."

This is also the view of **Satya** <note>An ancient authority often cited by Varahamihira</note>:

> "**Kemadruma** occurs in the absence of Sunapha, Anapha, and Durudhara."

And further:

> "The **Sunapha** and **Anapha** combinations, and the **Durudhara**, arise from the houses occupied by the Moon, from the lords of the planets being in the front (2nd), back (12th), or both, excluding the Sun. Otherwise, the combination here is **Kemadruma**, where the birth is considered contemptible."

Some say "in the angles or the **Navamshas**" <term>Navamsha: the 1/9th divisional chart</term>. Certain teachers describe these three combinations as occurring in the angles, and some in the Navamshas. Thus, the Sunapha and other combinations are explained by planets staying in the second, twelfth, or both from the Moon. Similarly, by others such as **Shrutakirti** and **Jivasharma**...
